Course Objective:
To give an intensive introduction to an unfamiliar period and/or approach to the study of history;

To offer experience in the history and debates about sub-Saharan Africa and the world since 1800;

To develop skills in analysing historiography; and

To develop core skills such as: bibliographical search techniques; source analysis; essay writing; giving presentations; and, undertaking independent research.

Students who complete this module successfully will:

Acquire insight into the history, historiography, and debates about the historical relationship between sub-Saharan Africa and the world since 1800;

Comprehend how incorporation into/ participation in global networks has shaped sub-Saharan African societies over time.

Work with primary and secondary sources, applying appropriate concepts and (digital) methodological tools;

Effectively communicate their ideas in oral form, participating actively in class, preparing group presentations, and coordinating class discussions;

Develop their academic writing skills, by preparing a book review, a primary source analysis, and a research paper based on primary and secondary sources.

Course Content:
Africans and people for whom Africa has been a critical point of reference are actors on the world scene and have been for a long time. For this reason, sub-Saharan African countries, institutions, people, and economies are intertwined with the world in many ways. Its recent history has mostly been characterized by, among other things, violent conflict, abject poverty and governmental mismanagement. Despite its long painful and tragic engagement with the world, sub-Saharan Africa is probably one of the most misunderstood and misrepresented regions in the modern world. This module utilizes sub-Saharan Africa as a starting point from which to explore the spatial, technological, political and socio-economic location of Africa in global networks since 1800, and demonstrate how this has had an impact on sub-Saharan Africa. It seeks to inculcate a productive understanding of Africa’s place (past and present) in the world. Special attention is given to the dynamics that produced generations of African facilitators, as Joseph Miller has argued, “from the suppliers of slaves through post-colonial “gatekeeping” elites brokering flows of funds and commodities between national economies and international capital, often to their and their clients’ personal advantage.” An understanding of the relationship between sub-Saharan Africa and the world enriches understanding of both global connections and specific regional, sub-regional and local contexts. Crucially, it encourages students to assess how Africans shaped as well as experienced such engagements.

Teaching Methods:
2 Seminars (4 hours per week) plus work in archives, independent and assisted by teachers (scheduled moments)

Method of Assessment:
Participation in class (10%)

Book review (20%)

a primary source analysis (10%)

a research pitch: an oral presentation of the research paper (10%)

Research paper (50%)

Format: The teacher will provide a list of texts that students can select. Students are also allowed to suggest their own preferred texts. Within the broader theme, the reading list will be adapted to fit the interests and needs of the students who participate.

Meetings: weekly, by appointment.

Reading list as discussed with students (ca. 600 pages)

Course Objective:
At the end of the course students can:

Understand key political, social and cultural debates and analytical concepts in the history and anthropology of the Maghreb.

Interpret and assess a selection of (translated) primary sources (e.g. archival sources, ethnographies, oral traditions and oral histories, documentary films) relevant to the course topics.

Reflect on key (sensitive) scholarly debates regarding migration, gender, colonialism, nationalism, and religion in the Maghreb and take up an informed position on them.

Course Content:
This course introduces students to key debates in the history and anthropology of the Maghreb (with emphasis on Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia), while continuously connecting the region to world history at large. The course reflects on the history of both disciplines in the region and offers critical insights into the construction of historical and ethnographic knowledge. It provides insight into political, social, and cultural issues that have caught the attention of historians and anthropologists, such as Islam and religious minorities, gender, colonialism and the colonial legacy, nationalism, language and ethnicity, migration and development, and revolts and revolutions.

Teaching Methods:
Lectures and seminars, 4 contact hours in total per week. Students should come to class prepared to actively discuss sources and readings.

Method of Assessment:
Written exam (closed book)

Literature:
A reading list of mandatory articles will be distributed at the beginning of the course.

Recommended reading: P.C. Naylor, North Africa : a history from antiquity to the present (University of Texas Press 2015, Revised edition)

Target Audience:
This course is an elective for BA 2 students Geschiedenis and BA2 students History and International Studies. The course is also open to BA2/3 students in Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology, Political Science, and Theology and Religious Studies. Exchange students should have a background in any of these fields.

Course Objective:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:

acquire knowledge of and develop insight into the approaches, concepts, and historiography of Global History, with particular reference to the worldwide development of capitalism and its influence on the development of social inequality

place and analyze historical themes in diachronic and geographical context, and engage with different approaches to the history of capitalism

critically approach dominant historical narratives and connect global with local developments

link the global history of capitalism to local processes, including the social and economic development of the Netherlands over the last 1000 years

formulate a research question on a specific theme from economic history and report on it clearly

develop the ability to independently find and integrate additional academic literature

work effectively with academic books and articles and draw connections between a case study and a broader academic framework

critically evaluate literature, theories, and opinions within the field and engage with normative approaches in academic thinking

Course Content:
Major social themes in the present — from globalization and economic growth to the rise or decline of social inequality, from climate change to the emergence of the platform economy — can only be properly understood when placed in the context of the global history of capitalism. This course examines the process of economic change in the world and in the Netherlands from approximately 1000 CE onward, in relation to its ecological, socio-political, and socio-cultural consequences. Central to the course are the fundamental problems of the acquisition and distribution of income, the formation and distribution of power, and the risks of human existence.

The history of capitalism has since the eighteenth century always been the terrain of social analysis and social critique. The course discusses the most important debates, theories, concepts, and approaches in global economic, ecological, and social history, with particular emphasis on the intensive study of academic literature.

Teaching Methods:
The course consists of lectures and seminars. Classes are scheduled twice a week. All sessions are compulsory. Students may be absent a maximum of two times, provided this is reported in advance with a valid reason. In case of more than two absences, access to the examination may be denied.

Method of Assessment:
The final grade for the course is determined by three components.

Active participation in the graded seminars. Students are assessed on their knowledge of the assigned literature and their substantive contribution to discussion.

A midterm exam tests knowledge and understanding of the historiographical debates and theoretical frameworks covered in the first half of the course.

A final research paper requires students to apply the concepts and approaches studied in the course to a specific historical theme, drawing on both the course literature and independently found academic sources.

Conditions for passing the course and the possibilities for resits will be specified in the course manual available on Canvas at the start of the course.

Literature:
The course is based on a selection of academic books and articles covering major debates in global economic and social history. The full list of required literature will be made available on Canvas at the start of the course.

Course Objective:
This course is an introduction to environmental history, also called ecological history. We devote special attention to the historical challenges regarding Water, Animals, Energy and Climate and we addressing questions about the agency of nature in history. The learning objectives are: Applying source criticism and conducting source analysis, Close en distant reading of sources and literature, Reviewing literature through comparing articles, Freely reflecting on a historical topic, making a comment, Presenting research findings and arguments orally and in writing.

Course Content:
In this course we focus on the complex historical relationship between humans and nature. It is connected to large global processes like population growth, industrialization, technological and scientific change, urbanization, and changes in consumption patterns. Humans contributed to large changes in the natural environment including pollution, desertification, reclamation of landscapes, decrease of biodiversity, exhaustion of natural resources, and climate change. How did the interdependency or entanglement of humans and nature develop over time? In addition, we will problematize the role of nature in history, in order to sharpen our focus. We devote special attention to the historical challenges regarding Water, Animals, Energy and Climate. Water is essential for producing drinking water and in industrial processes (groundwater, rainwater, surface water) and an important means of transport (canals, rivers, seas). But water can also be a safety threat. Flooding can endanger lives, but drought can do that too. Also controlling water may be an expression of political power or a political goal by itself. We concentrate on the period 1800-2000, when we changed from organic to fossil fuels and populations exploded worldwide. We compare developments in global regions, in particular Europe, USA, Asia, Australia, and South Africa.

Teaching Methods:
Weekly: lecture 2hrs, tutorial 2 hrs, 1 outdoor excursion if the weather permits. For all presence mandatory.

Method of Assessment:
The total grade of the course is the weighted average of the assignments (40%) and exam (60%). The exam grade must be at least a 6 in order to get a pass for the course. The exam is similar to the assignments. You will read a text, answer open questions and you write a short essay where you can apply theories and concepts learned in the course.

Literature:
All literature will be provided in Canvas.

Target Audience:
Other thant history students are welcome, but need to contact the lecturer before the course to check if they have sufficient background.

Course Objective:
The aim of this course is to introduce students to the richness of modern Southeast Asian history, placing it within global histories of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Southeast Asia's historical entanglement with Europe through colonialism, decolonisation and 'Cold' War politics is a particular focus of this course. Students will be introduced in this course to sources from, and narratives and debates about, key themes from modern Southeast Asian history. Students will learn to identify the global nature of Southeast Asia's history, but also to appreciate important local variations in how colonialism was established, contested, and dismantled in different contexts, and what nation-building in postcolonial Southeast Asia has entailed. Particularly, students will learn:

Familiarity with major themes in modern Southeast Asian history.

To understand the importance of perspective, genre, audience and function in assessing primary sources from Southeast Asia - particularly where those sources were made by Europeans there.

To be able to identify and evaluate key historiographical debates in modern Southeast Asian history.

To formulate an argument or position about major topics in Southeast Asian history, and their relevance to the present.

Classes will consist of lectures and seminars. Assignments will be structured around primary source analysis and building critical argumentation skills. Students will be given primary sources to analyse, and exposure to various methodologies for approaching a variety of sources (in English translation, or in visual or material media). Students will also learn to critically assess secondary sources.

Course Content:
This course will introduce students to the richness and complexity of modern Southeast Asian history, placing it within global histories of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Southeast Asia has historically been at the centre of modern histories of globalisation. Its geographic location has placed it at the crossroads of global trade and strategic conflicts. Its natural wealth has made it a major source of global commodities. The world's major religions - Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism and Christianity - have made Southeast Asia a site of pilgrimage, learning and adaptation. Modern Southeast Asia has a long history of European colonialism, which has left powerful legacies in the region and a complex inheritance for Europe, including the Netherlands. Southeast Asia was occupied by Japan during World War Two, and then was one of the first regions to decolonise in the aftermath. The Cold War was actually a series of 'hot' wars in Southeast Asia. Communism, nationalism, non-alignment, democratisation and authoritarianism have all been part of the region's twentieth century history.

Students will develop specialised area studies knowledge on Southeast Asia, and enhance their research skills for historians.

Teaching Methods:
Classes are weekly for the duration of the course. They include lectures, and seminars where attendance is mandatory.

This course is taught in English. Students are welcome to submit written assignments in English or Dutch.

Method of Assessment:
Primary source analysis (30%)

Participation (20%)

Oral presentations (20%)

Exams (30%)

Literature:
Reading list will be placed on canvas at the start of the course.

Course Objective:
The Digital Historian introduces second-year History students to the theories, debates, methods, and infrastructures of digital history and digital humanities. Combining critical reflection with hands-on practice, the course explores how historical sources are digitised, organised, searched, analysed, preserved, and presented in digital environments. Students engage with key themes in digital humanities and digital history, including metadata, digitisation, text analysis, mapping, public history, digital infrastructures, ethics, and artificial intelligence. Through lectures, seminars, excursions, and collaborative project work, students develop both practical skills and a critical understanding of what it means to practise history in the digital age.

Course Content:
This course is organised around three interconnected dimensions: debates, sources & methods, and infrastructures. Each teaching day combines conceptual

framing with guided practice, so that students connect digital outputs to historical interpretation. The excursions are embedded in the course logic rather than

treated as add-ons: the archive visit foregrounds source mediation, while the data centre visit foregrounds material and institutional infrastructure.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. Explain key concepts and debates in digital history and digital humanities.

2. Critically assess the opportunities and limitations of digital methods for historical research.

3. Analyse how digitisation, metadata, and platforms shape historical sources and interpretation.

4. Apply selected digital methods to a historical question or source set.

5. Interpret digital outputs as historical arguments rather than neutral results.

6. Reflect on the ethical, material, institutional, political, and environmental dimensions of digital history.

7. Collaborate effectively in a small team on a digital history project.

8. Document and reflect on their learning in an individual portfolio.

Teaching Methods:
Contact hours (lectures, seminars, excursions, presentations): 28

Reading and preparation: 80

Seminar/lab preparation and follow-up: 20

Group project work: 20

Portfolio writing: 20

Method of Assessment:
Project portfolio (40%): Small-group project with presentation on project output or prototype, and a short methodology statement.
Individual portfolio (50%): Portfolio including reflections on both excursions and a final synthesis essay.
Attendance, Engagement & Participation (10%): Attendance, seminar engagement, workshop preparation, and participation in peer feedback and excursions.

Target Audience:
The Digital Historian is a compulsory second-year BA History course that introduces students to the theories, debates, methods, and infrastructures of digital history. In an intensive two-week format, students explore digitisation, metadata, text analysis, mapping, digital public history, infrastructure, ethics, and AI through lectures, workshops, and excursions. A visit to a digital archive and a visit to a data centre foreground the material and institutional dimensions of digital historical knowledge. Assessment combines a group digital history project with an individual reflective portfolio.

Course Objective:
The main goal of this course is to familiarize diverse group of students coming from different countries and educational backgrounds with some core aspects of the history of the Netherlands and of the way the Netherlands is imagined.

Students will also learn how to connect Dutch history with a number of present-day academic as well as public debates on issues such as national identity, tolerance, environment, colonialism, World War II, democracy and multiculturalism. They will learn how to critically connect these themes to different representations of Dutch history in the media, in museums and the internet.

As this course is open to non-history students, it will also introduce several concepts of history as an academic discipline, by discussing subfields of history such as political history, colonial history, environmental history and national history.

After taking this course, students will be able to recognize normative thinking in academic literature and in the work of historians, to read and summarize academic writing, to use scientific literature in debates and to critically addresses historical information and images.

Course Content:
Often, the perception of the Netherlands at home and abroad is ridden with stereotypes. It is a country of cheese, herring and coffeeshops. Canals, clogs, windmills and a very liberal attitude to life choices are also elements in this imagery. The struggle against water is yet another recurring theme in the way the Dutch are perceived and see themselves.

The course will cover a period of over 500 years from 1500 until the present, giving an overview of the multiple histories of the Netherlands. Besides written texts, audio-visual sources will also be employed in order to illuminate the themes that will be discussed. Breaking away from the Spanish Habsburg Empire in the late sixteenth century, the Dutch Republic became a world power in the course of the seventeenth century. As a republic it was an exception in an age of kingdoms and empires. The seventeenth century was marked by economic, scientific and cultural success. The foundations for a large colonial empire were laid in the seventeenth century. This period has been coined the ‘Golden Age’, a term that has come under scrutiny and debate in recent years. In the course the emergence of the Dutch Republic and the way the ‘Golden Age’ came into being and is remembered will be discussed. Several characteristics that are considered ‘typically Dutch’ such as a pragmatic, entrepreneurial mentality are linked to this period The merchant and the minister are two other images that are often used in characterizing the Dutch. As a country dependent on trade, international relations have always been of the utmost importance. As a small nation the Netherlands also has a tradition in international law as well as a tendency to imagine itself as holding the moral high-ground and a guide to the world.

During the course among others the following themes will be discussed:

The emergence of the Netherlands as an independent political nation and its development as a Republic in the seventeenth century

Notions of tolerance and religious diversity

The economic, scientific and cultural developments in the Netherlands (Rembrandt, Hugio Grotius)

The Dutch and water: a maritime power at sea, managing water at home

The Dutch as a colonial power and a post-colonial society

The transition from a Republic to a Kingdom

Pillarrized consensus democracy and present-day Dutch politics

The Dutch and the World Wars

Migration, diversity and race In the Netherlands

Discussion among students about the content of the lectures and the course literature is part of this course, which is specifically designed to connect history with contemporary issues. Quizzes and polls will be employed to stimulate class engagement.

Teaching Methods:
In period 1,each week there will be two lectures All the thematic lectures will be given by various lectures, primarily from the History Department of the VU. Presence in class is mandatory. Students who have a reason to be absent have to inform the course coordinator in time of their absence, which is limited to a maximum of two times, after which the student can be penalized with exclusion from participating in the exams.

Method of Assessment:
There is one written assignments (25%), as well as a written exam (75 %).

Literature:
Handbook: Kennedy, J. C. (2017). A concise history of the Netherlands. Cambridge University Press.

Students will also be asked to read additional articles or book chapters related to each theme, which will be posted on Canvas in due time.

Target Audience:
This course is open to students taking part in the minor programme 'History' or the programme 'A Semester in Amsterdam'; other exchange students and Dutch students interested in Dutch History.

Remarks:
This course will be provided two times during the academic year in period 1 (L_GCBAALG003) and in periods 4&5 (L_GCBAALG004).
All the lectures will be in English. Students who follow a Dutch language program can make their assignments in Dutch.

Course Objective:
At the end of the course the student will have gained insight into the historical development, internal dynamics, positioning within the city, and the image-formation of the Jewish culture and population of Amsterdam from 1600 to the present day. The student will be familiar with the most important sources, theories, and historiography on Amsterdam and Dutch Jewish history, and with the world-famous Amsterdam Jewish heritage institutions. The student will be able to contextualize, compare, and contrast Amsterdam and Dutch Jewish history within larger trends in Jewish and minority histories.

Course Content:
Amsterdam developed into the largest Jewish metropolis of Europe in the eighteenth century, making it a compelling case for studying the urban and cultural history of Jews in Europe and beyond. The image of Amsterdam as a 'Jewish City' — Mokum — has since become deeply embedded in the city's identity.

This interdisciplinary course traces the historical development of Amsterdam's Jewish communities across six themes: (1) the Sephardi 'Portuguese Nation': the Iberian conversos who settled in Amsterdam around 1600, reclaimed or converted to Judaism, and constructed a complex identity; (2) the Ashkenazi 'High German Nation': the rapidly growing migrant community of Central and East European Jews; (3) processes of segregation, concentration, and integration; (4) processes of identification as both part of and apart from Dutch society; (5) transnational connections through European, trans-Atlantic, and colonial networks; (6) the impact of the Holocaust and the reconstruction of postwar Jewish life.

Excursions and visits to Jewish heritage institutions — including the Jewish Historical Museum, Portuguese Synagogue, Ets Haim Library, Jewish Cemetery, and a walking tour of the historic Jewish quarter — are an integral part of the program. Students should expect some additional costs for admission and travel.

Teaching Methods:
Seminar and excursions. Attendance is mandatory. More than three unexcused absences will result in a failing grade.

Method of Assessment:
Podcast (25%), attendance (15%), and in-person written exam (60%).

Literature:
Blom, J. C. H., Renate G. Fuks-Mansfeld, and I. Schöffer. The History of the Jews in the Netherlands. Translated by Arnold J. Pomerans and Erica Pomerans. Oxford: Littman Library, 2002.

Additional readings will be posted on Canvas.

Target Audience:
The course is open to exchange and Dutch students with an interest in Amsterdam, urban history, Jews and Judaism, cultural history, and art and architectural history. Students enrolled in the Master Heritage Studies (Erfgoed) are also welcome — they can attend the seminars and excursions and incorporate their own research as 'Individuele Verdieping'.

Remarks:
This course is part of the minor 'European Urban and Cultural History.'

Excursions are a vital component of the course and may involve additional costs for museum admission and transport within Amsterdam. A museumjaarkaart or student discount card is recommended. Course Objective:

Course Content:
Origins of History: The Globalizing Mediterranean World 3500 BCE–1000 CE (minor)

In this course, we will explore the globalising world of ancient West Asia, Egypt, Greece, and Rome, examining developments in these regions up until the year 1000 CE. From the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, we witness the emergence of complex societies that used writing in Mesopotamia and Egypt, as well as the expansion of territorial states and empires. We then turn to the Greek world and the rise and fall of the Roman Empire, before moving on to Late Antiquity, the advent of Islam, and the early Middle Ages. Throughout the course, we will also examine the economic and social relations within these societies, as well as their cultural, political, and religious institutions. All of these factors were influenced by the increasing connectivity between different geographical regions.

Teaching Methods:
Lectures, seminars.

Method of Assessment:
Written examination. A resit takes place in the next period.

Literature:
For students of the History and International Studies track:
L. de Blois & R.J. van der Spek, An Introduction to the Ancient World. Third edition, London & New York: Routledge 2019.

For students of the Geschiedenis track:
L. de Blois & R.J. van der Spek, Een kennismaking met de oude wereld, Bussum: Coutinho 2017.

Target Audience:
Part of the Culture of the Ancient World minor programme. Also recommended to other students with a serious interest in ancient history.

Course Content:
Subject: Religious Change and Conflict in the Fourth and Fifth Centuries (preliminary description)

The fourth century witnessed a significant transformation in the religious landscape of the Roman Empire. Following Constantine's conversion and rise to power, Christianity gained increasing prominence. Many people followed his example and converted. However, there was also opposition from adherents of the traditional Graeco-Roman cults. Inevitably, this led to conflict. First, we will examine the measures Constantine took against traditional religions. Regarding the 'pagan' reaction, we will examine the case of Julian, Constantine's nephew. Having left the religion his uncle had embraced, he tried to halt the advance of Christianity. We will see that Graeco-Roman religions also developed during this period. Finally, we will examine the process of Christianization in cities such as Gaza, where traditional cults had always been strong, and we will explore how internal conflicts within Christianity led to the separation of the Church in Persia from that in the Roman Empire.

Course Objective:
The course aims to situate China in the history of the modern world, highlighting how key developments in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were linked to broader trends in global history including colonialism, capitalism, and socialism. We will trace how shifts in international political and economic relations brought new goods, ideas, and social norms. In addition, we will discuss the political and public function of modern history in today’s China.

Course Content:
Students will learn about some of the main junctures of China's encounters with the modern world from the events leading up to the Opium War to its current central place in shaping global history. Concepts covered include comparative imperial history, sovereignty, extraterritoriality, nationalism, and globalisation. Students will also learn about ways in which history and heritage are currently mobilised by the Chinese government and how researchers dispute them.

Teaching Methods:

A closed-book midterm and a final oral exam.

Course Objective:
During this course and after completing it, students will:

develop a familiarity with the history of Latin America since the late eighteenth century.

acquire knowledge from (and critically assess) academic literature.

be able to recognize historiographical debates in the field.

apply historical knowledge acquired in previous courses to further examine the peculiarities of Latin American history in a global context.

understand and discuss primary sources (translated into English, in case of written sources) in their historical context.

use their historical knowledge to understand and take a critical stance in contemporary discussions in and about Latin America.

be able to effectively communicate their ideas in oral form.

further develop their academic writing skills, by preparing a final paper based on a critical historiographic survey

Course Content:
This course offers students an introduction to the history of modern Latin America. Starting with the period of revolutions that swept through the region in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, it discusses the main political, social, and economic developments that shaped its history in the last two centuries. Avoiding a juxtaposition of national cases and events, the course develops a global and transnational perspective that focuses on several crucial aspects, including the processes of state-building and economic transformation, the consequences of internal and international migrations and displacements, the development of nationalist and populist ideologies, the recurrence of military dictatorships, and the victories and defeats of revolutionary movements. Moreover, it pays particular attention to the relationship between Latin America and other regions of the world, in particular Western Europe and the United States.

Teaching Methods:
Two sessions per week. Students should come to the meetings prepared to actively discuss the readings.

Method of Assessment:
The final grade for the course is determined by three components.

Graded seminars. Students are assessed on their knowledge of the texts and their active, substantive contribution to the discussion.

A primary source analysis. Students find, identify, analyse, and contextualise a visual primary source from Latin America, drawing on both course readings and independently found academic literature.

A final written exam. Students answer a selection of essay questions covering topics from across the course, demonstrating knowledge of the relevant historical developments and engaging analytically with the literature discussed in class. A passing grade on the final exam is required to pass the course.

Further details on deadlines, word counts, and assessment criteria will be specified in the course manual available on Canvas at the start of the course.

Literature:
Chasteen, John C. Born in Blood & Fire: A Concise History of Latin America. Fourth edition. New York: W.W. Norton & Company, 2016.

Students will also read a selection of book chapters, articles, and primary sources that will be available via the VU Library and/or in Canvas.

Additionally, students will be encouraged to discuss a selection of Latin American films, music, art, and literature.

Course Objective:
Students can:

demonstrate historical-political trajectories that constitute contemporary Middle East,

analytically debate Orientalism and engage with misrepresentations of the Middle East through works of revolutionary/social justice-oriented thinkers from Nazik Al-Abid, Abdul Rahman Al-Kawakibi to Edward Said and from the Middle East.

define the notion of Empire as a mode of persistent domination that remains in effect in the Middle East.

Course Content:
In the midst of what ICJ called a plausible genocide in Gaza, some in the Global North said, 'the situation in the Middle East should not divide us'; however, the question remains: what and where is this Middle East? This course addresses these questions by diving into the Middle East's historiographies, histories and memories to open up its political-historical construction. The course discusses how past and present influence the armed conflicts in the Middle East and how historiographies have shaped the dominant imagination of the Global North about the peoples of the Middle East.

This course unpacks the notion of Empire and Dispossession through revolutionary thinkers whose criticism of colonialism shaped colonial struggles against French and British mandates in the Middle East and their legacy have enabled resistance against Middle Eastern authoritarian regimes and also Israel as the ongoing colonial settler project. Furthermore, it shows Empire is mode of persistent domination that impacts of decolonized nations through cultural framing, Racialisations and border regimes.

This course engages with Middle Eastern thinkers such as Nazik Al-Abid, Abdul Rahman Al-Kawakibi to Edward Said to introduce Orientalism and Islamophobic framing of Muslims and peoples of the contemporary Middle East. The course also discusses Racism and Aryanism within the Middle East (the case of Iran), and it ends by engaging the cultural politics of images, visuals, aesthetics and objects in and from the Middle East.

This course operates through academic dialogues that begin from the point of view of dispossessed and colonised peoples such as Palestinians and engages with literature that radically criticised and dismantled perspectives of the Dominant.

Teaching Methods:
This course partially uses the flipping classroom method, which means students receive content in advance and discuss it in class during group discussions or in conversations with the teacher. Attendance is mandatory, and students missing two lectures will be given extra assignments and tasks to compensate for their absence. Students missing three lectures will not be allowed to finish the course.

Method of Assessment:
Writing assessment

Group Presentation

Course Objective:
After completing the course, students are able to:

Explain how social media platform features (e.g. affordances, interaction mechanisms) influence language use and communication practices;

Analyse linguistic features of social media discourse (e.g. style, tone, interaction patterns) using concepts from linguistics and discourse analysis;

Evaluate how linguistic choices affect interaction, engagement, and the visibility of content on social media;

Examine and interpret how information circulates across platforms and audiences, and how language changes or remains stable in this process;

Design and conduct a small-scale empirical study of social media language, and present the findings in a clear and well-structured manner.

Course Content:
Social media have transformed how people use language: we use emojis to express emotion, hashtags to organize content, and comments to respond to others in real time.

In this course, we explore how language functions in these digital environments. We examine how platform features, such as character limits and affordances for interaction, influence how individuals and organisations communicate online. We also look at how how linguistic choices themselves shape interaction and engagement: how language invites responses, fosters connection, or helps content gain visibility. Furthermore, we examine how information circulates across platforms, for instance when information is posted across different platforms or to different audiences.

Building on your prior knowledge of linguistics, discourse analysis, and communication studies, you will learn to analyse language as it is actually used on social media platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, and Reddit. You will apply analytical tools to authentic examples, focusing on features such as style, tone, interaction patterns, and recurring forms of expression. Through this, you will gain insight into what makes language use in social media distinct from other forms of communication.

The course places a strong emphasis on hands-on analysis and critical reflection. You will work with real data, develop your own observations, and connect them to theoretical and empirical insights from the literature. By doing so, you will not only better understand how language operates in social media, but also learn how to study it in a systematic, evidence-based way.

Teaching Methods:
One lecture and one seminar (mandatory attendance) per week in period 5.

In period 6, students will work on a small-scale research project in weekly seminars (mandatory attendance).

Method of Assessment:
Assessment consists of a combination of one or multiple individual assignments (50%; assessment of learning objectives1-4) and one or multiple group assignment (50%; assessment of learning objectives 2-5).

Participation in the seminars is mandatory (pass/fail).
All assignments should be graded with minimally 5.5 out of 10 points.

To pass the course, all assignments must be marked complete (‘pass’ OR a minimum of 5.5 out of 10 points). Grades will be published on Canvas. If you fail one or more assignments, you must take a re-sit for the assignment(s).

Course Objective:
After completion of this course:

you can describe the most important principles of inductive, data-driven research as it is done in the field of conversation analysis;

you can recognize the basic concepts used to analyze language use in social interaction; and

you are able to apply these basic concepts to analyze natural language use in different settings.

Course Content:
This course starts from the idea that spoken and written discourse can be studied as social action: when interacting with each other via different modes of communication, people manage to accomplish a variety of actions, such as inviting or blaming, accounting or denying matters.

This course aims to develop your analytical skills to understand what it is exactly that people do when they talk in person or over the phone. You will also encounter other examples such as broadcast interviews. The focus across settings and modes of communication will be to examine how speakers accomplish whatever it is they are doing and how this influences the unfolding conversation. The analytical skills are based on the concepts and principles used in conversation analysis and reflect current research.

You will analyze instances of informal talk as well as talk in institutional or organizational settings. Data for analysis might thus be derived from various settings and contain both instances of spoken interaction as well as mediated discourse.

When you pass this course, you are able to break down any conversation in turns, ascribe social actions to these turns by asking and developing claims on what would be an appropriate response to what the conversational partner has done in the previous turn. This procedure helps you to see how turns at talk drive conversations. You will be able to use these analytical skills to evaluate and offer advice on the options speakers have at different moment in the interaction and how this has an influence on the course of the conversation, whatever mode of communication they employ. Based on these observations, you are able to formulate ideas on which turns at talk are more appropriate or desirable in the given context.

Teaching Methods:
Lecture, seminars and workshops, 6 hours per week in total.

Method of Assessment:
Written exam (55%); assessment of learning objectives 1-3

Research assignment (45%); assessment of learning objectives 2-3

Course Objective:
Upon completion of the course, students:

Have obtained insight into the (social-)scientific theories and empirical findings regarding message use and effects on social media, including electronic word of mouth and webcare;

Can apply theories about language use and communicative effects in social media to case studies;

Can formulate social media strategies on the basis of (social-)scientific theories and empirical findings;

Can collect and analyze social media messages for linguistic (and visual) features;

Can report on the results of a small-scale content-analytical social media study in a scientific report.

Course Content:
In online settings, consumers are able to voice their complaints, questions, and remarks to a larger audience. For instance, consumers post a negative review of their restaurant visit on Tripadvisor or post about their positive experience with an electronic device they recently ordered on Google. The process of electronic word of mouth amplifies these messages and can have consequences for companies' brand reputations.

To manage the potential negative impact of dissatisfied customer experiences, organizations have appointed organizational representatives to monitor the online interactions (i.e., who is talking with what sentiment(s) about our organization/products/services?). When deemed necessary, these representatives intervene by responding to questions, complaints, and compliments. Such practices have become known as webcare.

Recently, webcare has become a topic of interest in scientific research. There have been numerous experimental studies in which the effects of specific webcare interventions are examined. But it is still unclear which determinants play a role in this process and which (psychological, linguistic, interpersonal) theoretical models can be related to the phenomenon.

This course teaches the theoretical principles related to online phenomena such as electronic word of mouth (eWOM) and webcare. It also provides students hands-on experience in monitoring, analyzing, and reporting a research project about the language of social media by introducing them to the research method of content analysis.

Teaching Methods:
Each week for six weeks, there will be lectures and one seminar.

During the interactive lectures, recent theoretical and empirical studies investigating the role of language in social media are discussed. Special attention will be paid to methodological aspects of these studies. During the seminars, students will work on a group assignment in which they collect, analyze and report on a research project that examines the linguistic features of social media messages.

Attendance is mandatory for the seminar meetings, and highly recommended for the lectures.

Method of Assessment:
A written exam (50%; course objectives 1-3) and a group assignment consisting of sub assignments with a small individual component (50%; course objectives 3-5).

To pass the course, you need to obtain a minimum grade of 5.5 our of 10 for the written exam, as well as for the group assignment.

Course Objective:
To acquire knowledge of processing verbal and visual messages, and especially their interactions;

To learn the fundamental cognitive principles behind visual metaphors in advertising and other persuasive communication, and the interplay of text and visuals in instructional communication;

To investigate communication messages with appropriate research methods; and

To apply learned knowledge to well-reasoned assessment of communication messages.

Course Content:
Images are becoming more and more important in communication messages. Dependent on communicative goals, both the design and function of images in documents may differ. In three themes we will consider how images are processed differently by viewers due to other functions they serve. We will look at visual metaphors in advertising and their persuasive function. We will also study the how visual and verbal content comes together in learning contexts. In both cases, the interplay of images with text plays a pivotal role. Theories of information processing will be studied and applied to analyze the role of images in documents and the intended and unintended effects they may have on document users.

Literary texts will be related to other cultural products and to their historical, political and philosophical background. The concept of the 'Golden Age' will be critically scrutinized.

Course Objective:
In this course, students are trained in the computational analysis of texts through various approaches: rule-based systems, supervised machine learning methods, and prompt-based text analysis using Large Language Models such as LLaMA. Students learn to design and refine their own experiments and critically evaluate the reliability of the generated analyses.In particular, we explore the process of identifying and annotating information in both historical and contemporary texts. A strong emphasis is placed on assessing the reliability of these methods in relation to specific research questions.

Learning goals:

At the end of this course students will be able to (1) Explain the importance of systematic evaluation methodologies for assessing the performance and reliability of computational tools. (2) Demonstrate a basic understanding of rule-based, supervised machine learning, and prompt-based approaches, including their underlying principles, strengths, limitations, and appropriate application contexts. (3) Run automatic methods for text analysis (4) Construct and curate a test set that aligns with a defined research question and supports reliable and valid tool evaluation. (5) Design, implement, and conduct an inter-annotator agreement analysis to assess annotation consistency and reliability. (6) Develop and execute an evaluation experiment. (7) Evaluate and interpret the performance of the evaluation experiment using appropriate evaluation metrics. (8) Present tbeir findings in a written report

Course Content:
In recent decades, NLP (Natural Language Processing) approaches have become widely used by researchers in the humanities and social sciences. This course explores how computational methods can be applied to text analysis, while maintaining a critical perspective on what these tools actually do — and how much we can trust their results.

Rather than treating NLP systems as mysterious black boxes, students learn to experiment with, compare, and systematically evaluate different approaches to text analysis. The course covers prompt-based analysis with Large Language Models such as LLaMA, rule-based methods, and potentially supervised machine learning approaches. Students will not only learn how to apply these methods, but also how to investigate their strengths, weaknesses, and suitability for specific research questions.

A central theme of the course is evaluation. How do we know whether a model performs well? When can we trust its output, and when should we be skeptical? Students learn to assess model performance through quantitative evaluation using standard metrics, as well as qualitative error analysis that uncovers recurring mistakes and points toward possible improvements. The course combines hands-on experimentation with critical reflection on the use of AI and NLP in research practice.

Teaching Methods:
Lectures, Work groups, Practical sessions (2 * 1,5 hrs each week) Attendance is mandatory.

Method of Assessment:
The course includes three bi-weekly group and individual assignment components (learning objectives 1,3, 4,5, 6,7), a midterm exam (1, 2, 7), and a final report (3,6,7,8). All graded components must receive a minimum grade of 5.5.

understand core concepts within cognitive linguistics and their implications for language learning/teaching

analyze language data using cognitive linguistic frameworks

Course Content:
How can a house burn up as it burns down? Why does an alarm go off when it is on? Non-native speakers struggle with these frustrating constructions. But there is a way through the wilderness: many seemingly arbitrary facets of language are in fact motivated and meaningful. This course introduces students to cognitive linguistics - a usage-based, meaning-centered approach to language – and its applied potential in educational contexts (e.g., vocabulary development, grammar instruction, raising language awareness.) Students will understand the core concepts within cognitive linguistics and put their knowledge into action by designing concrete learning activities.

Illustrate core concepts and terminology in morphology and syntax, and morphosyntactic interface;

describe syntactic structures such as phrases, clauses, and constituent relations;

analyze morphemes, word formation processes, and grammatical categories in linguistic data;

analyze morphological and syntactic similarities and differences across languages, and reflect on linguistic variation based on own analysis;

construct syntactic structures using standard linguistic notations and principles.

Course Content:
This course is an introductory course in the fields of morphology and syntax. It provides students with a foundation in these two core domains of linguistics that focus on the structure of words and sentences and on the interface between these two. Students will be introduced to key concepts and terminology used in the analysis of language structures across languages. The course covers topics such as morphemes, word formation processes, grammatical categories, phrase structures, constituent analysis, and basic syntactic relations. Through lectures and practical exercises, students will learn how to identify and analyze morphological, syntactic and morphosyntactic patterns in language. The course also familiarizes students with basic argumentation and analytical skills used in linguistic research within the aforementioned fields.

Course Objective:
Knowledge and insight: 1.1 You will be able to identify the possible causes and the symptoms of dyslexia. 1.2 You will be able to describe how the screening and diagnostic process takes place and what efficient treatment methods look like. 1.3 You will be able to compare the situation of children with dyslexia across languages. 1.4 You will be able to interpret research outcomes described in academic publications.

Course Content:
About 7% of all people in the world have dyslexia. These people have trouble learning how to read and write. Many different treatment methods (some more effective than others) have been developed over the last decades. Treatment helps people with dyslexia to better understand the orthography of their own language and how to strategically put that knowledge to use, while reading or writing. However, dyslexia cannot be cured, so it will affect their lives, whether it concerns a child going to school or an adult working in a professional setting.

We will study literature about the assumed causes of dyslexia and the (linguistic) theories that aim at confirming these assumptions. We will also study the Dutch educational system and the ways in which it has incorporated structural measures to identify dyslexia markers in children as early as possible. Besides that, we will study screening materials, the phases of the diagnostic process, and treatment methods. We will analyse written data from children with dyslexia. During the second half of the course, students will give a presentation (individual or in small groups) about a topic that was not yet (elaborately) treated in class.

Course Objective:
The aim of this course is to gain insights into the assessment of linguistic performances in children who acquire language and (adult) second language learners.

After this course, the student will be able to:

place the purpose of a language test within the theoretical construct of language proficiency;

assess the design of a language test using psychometric concepts such as validity and reliability.

relate the results of a language test to the social consequences associated with it.

Course Content:
Evaluating learning performances is a challenging and difficult task. Since we measure Language Proficiency and/or Language Development, we need to know what this construct is about, how it can be operationalized and how it can be measured. Based on the test results we can draw conclusions on both the reliability of the test and on the learner’s proficiency.

The focus of this course will be on the process of constructing language tests. This is a stepwise process during which theoretical and practical perspectives are discussed. Based on the construct of language proficiency/ language development, notions such as final attainment and proficiency levels, will be applied to (good) test items and finally, to a (good) language test.

Course Objective:
The student is expected to study and thereby gain insight into the different ways in which ancient Christianity developed. (S)he/They must be able to chart and understand the connections between the historical phenomena involved. This goal is achieved by way of a two-fold track. First, the student acquires knowledge based on primary sources, which are studied in translation. These sources, covering a variety of genres, are analysed and put into context. Secondly, an introductory text book on the field of early Christianity is studied (see course reading). Based on the literature the student must become aware of the different frameworks of interpretation which have been operative in recent years within the field. In view of this, attention is paid to scholarly debate including theories and models.

the ability to

communicate knowledge of the subject in written form (written exam).

Course Content:
During this course, the development of ancient Christianity will be studied in context. In the process, the formation of the Christian religious tradition will be approached from different angles, including socio-political, broadly cultural (including philosophical), and more specifically religious studies perspectives. Characteristics of the various historical phases within early Christianity as well as the most prominent conflicts during the first centuries of the common era will be discussed. In addition, attention will be paid to innovative literary genres and the authors who produced these. The related themes of material culture, artistic invention, and visual representation (significant identity markers) will also be addressed. As the course is taught in English, it is well suited to international students.

The international context of the field of early Christian studies will be in view as well.

Course Objective:
Course goal:

The focus of this course will be on Intercultural Philosophy. You will learn how philosophy helps to reflect on humanity and reality, in culturally differentiated ways.

Learning objectives:

You will get insight into how philosophers/philosophy help(s) to understand one’s own culture and that of others

You will acquire tools to critically question the claims to universal reason of ‘Western’ thinking

You are able to critically reflect on how your own cultural background influences your understanding

You can reflect in a philosophical manner, both collectively (in seminars) and individually (through assignments)

Course Content:
Philosophy is a discipline that focuses more on questions than answers. Examples of philosophical questions are: What is reality? What can human beings know? How do our academic frameworks steer our understanding? How does knowledge inform our practical life, and our morality?

In this course, we will focus on the intercultural aspects of philosophy, which center on the question of understanding. Human thinking is formed and rooted in cultures. These are not fixed, bounded wholes, but we are able to learn another culture from the inside by living in it, and can go back and forth through different cultures. How do we, however, translate between cultures? And how can we understand someone who is formed to think in another language, with different moral rules?

Due to colonialism, often in philosophy, Eurocentric philosophical traditions are centered while other forms of philosophy are neglected. From the end of the 20th century, German and Austrian philosophers have formed a school of Intercultural Philosophy as a way to address this. You will get acquainted with their approach, and with further developments of their thought by other philosophers. Using the intercultural philosophy approach, you will zoom in on the question of ‘Self-hood’ by reflecting on philosophies from African and Asian cultures.

Teaching Methods:

In the lectures, students will be introduced to the readings and get an overview of the context they are situated in. In the seminars, they will help each other, under the guidance of an experienced teaching assistant, to read the text material, critically evaluate its contents, and apply them to real world questions.

Course Content:
This course introduces into European philosophies of the 20th and 21th century, and aims at a better understanding of the most important themes and topics in this tradition. At large it is characterized by two lines of thought: the decentering of the subject and the linguistic turn. These developments are traceable in the most important philosophical schools of this period. Another important topic is the Enlightenment: many philosophers either relate to this historical period in the European history, or develop a novel notion of what it entails. A third characteristic is critique: most philosophers either develop a strong critique of our age or of the philosophical tradition, or both.

In the course, you will be introduced into these ideas and will read and discuss texts of important philosophers of the 20th and beginning of the 21th century.

The Masters of Suspicion (turn 19th/20th century): Nietzsche

Existentialism: Sartre and Beauvoir

Phenomenology: Heidegger

Political phenomenology: Arendt

Hermeneutics: Gadamer

Critical theory/Frankfurter Schule: Horkheimer and Adorno

Philosophy of difference: Deleuze

Post-structuralism: Foucault

Course Objective:
This course is an introduction to epistemology. The Course Learning Objectives are:

1. Analyze Philosophical Arguments: To practice and become more comfortable with identifying and evaluating arguments in epistemology.

2. Analyze Philosophical Concepts: To practice and become more comfortable with analyzing key concepts in epistemology using conceptual analysis; and to understand some of the limitations and controversies surround this method.

3. Explication and Explanation: To clearly state and explain key epistemological theories, their motivations, and certain key challenges from the course lectures and readings—i.e., to demonstrate awareness of what the major epistemological theories are, what motivations there is for them, and what some of the key challenges facing them are thought to be, drawing on the academic literature we read and explore in epistemology.

4. Defend Epistemological Views: To clearly state and defend one’s own educated epistemological views in written and verbal form—i.e., by connecting your own educated judgments with the academic literature we read in the course.

5. Apply Epistemology to Contemporary Issues: To apply key epistemological theories, arguments, and objections/replies to cases. This involves some command of many of the previous learning goals, and invites the development and application of your own creativity.

Course Content:
Epistemology is the philosophical study of knowledge, belief, truth, rationality, and their applications. It asks descriptive questions like "what is knowledge?" as well as normative questions, like "when should a person believe what someone tells them?" This course introduces students to fundamental concepts and key debates in contemporary epistemology, including some of its social, ethical, and political dimensions. We will address the following topics and questions, exploring the main theories and arguments devised to address them:

Theory of Knowledge: What is knowledge and what (if anything) is its value? What is the 'traditional' conception of knowledge and what (if anything) is wrong with it?

Philosophical analysis: How should we understand epistemological concepts — should they be conceptually analyzed? How do we do that?

Theory of Justification: What makes a belief justified or rational? Can you be rational in thinking what you do without knowing that your thinking is rational?

Skepticism: Can we refute skepticism? How?

Perception: How does perception give us knowledge and rational belief?

Testimony: How does testimony give us knowledge and rational belief?

Echo chambers: Can we escape echo chambers? Do filter bubbles make us more dogmatic?

Disagreement: Does peer disagreement render our moral, political, or religious beliefs unjustified?

Ethics of Belief: Are there 'bad' or wrongful beliefs? How can any beliefs be wrong if we can't chose what we believe?

You will gain knowledge of:

The basics of Intercultural and Postcolonial Approaches in doing Philosophy

And insight into:

Inclusive/exclusive power structures embedded in Western philosophy at the level of concepts, text and discourse.

The relation between inclusive/exclusive power structures in philosophy and social structures.

Think from non-Western dominated philosophical perspectives

Course Content:
Course Content:

This course studies the exclusionary effects of the Western philosophical canon, as well as efforts to repair them. Postcolonial Theory and Intercultural Philosophy represent two different approaches geared towards such repair. We will study them and some classic authors that created these approaches. We will look into their historical contexts, and analyze where they conflict and where they complement each other. We will do all of this by means of critical text-reading, group dialogue, and forming one’s own (argued) view of the course materials in writing.

The Western canon is a term we use for the body of philosophical work that self-identifies as rooted in ancient Greek philosophical thought and reached its pinnacle in the North-European Enlightenment. It is supposed to be most rational and has a universal reach to enlighten ‘all mankind’. The canon construed its own history of rational progress (Park 2013), while projecting an ’other’ to differentiate itself from. This other historically comprised a variety of thinkers from many parts of the world that may be sexualized (e.g. female thinkers’) racialized (as ‘black’ or ‘indian’) or culturalized (as Asian, African, indigenous native American, etc.).

Postcolonial Theory is the name for a body of critical thought that arose around the time of political decolonization and that persisted in the decades after up till now as a critique of neocolonial situations. It also includes critiques of racial oppression in its systemic forms.

Intercultural Philosophy has its roots in the increasing encounters between people through globalization, migration and communication by all kinds of different means. In Europe it had its systematic formulation in the 1990s and is based upon thinkers of dialogue such as Hans-Georg Gadamer. We will also study a new African approach, based upon the concept and practice of conversation.

Course Content:
Since the beginning of the 20th century, a new tradition in philosophy has emerged, which became known as analytic philosophy. This tradition is variously characterized by its conceptual rigor, tight argumentation, logical formalization, appeals to common sense, and (as the name suggests) attention for analysis. We will study the early development of this tradition in the first half of the 20th century. A historical overview of the major developments will be given, and we will read read primary texts by Frege, Russell, Moore, Wittgenstein, and Stebbing.

to introduce the text to be read in the next class.

Target Audience:
The course is for 2nd year Bachelor students in Philosophy.
The course can be followed by other students, but some knowledge of formal logic is required, as well as some background knowledge of epistemology, philosophy of science, and metaphysics.

Course Objective:
The aims of the course are to:

Introduce important metaphysical concepts, positions, and problems (lectures and readings).

Introduce contemporary questions and debates in metaphysics, broadly ‘analytical’ in style (lectures).

Familiarize students with a number of classic papers and contemporary readings in metaphysics (at-home reading).

Stimulate philosophical thinking about metaphysical problems and methods to resolve/dissolve them (assessment 1-2).

Course Content:
The course cover central topics in contemporary metaphysics:

Free will: do we have free will? How can free will co-exist with determinism? How could it co-exist with indeterminism?

Modality: (possibility and necessity). What does it mean for something to be possible? What does it mean for it is be necessary? Are there 'possible worlds?'—that is, do they really exist, just isolated from the actual world?

Personal Identity: What does it take to retain identity over time? What makes you you? Is personal identity a matter of psychological continuity, or having an immaterial soul?

Being and Nothing: why something rather nothing? Why something rather than nothing? Why does anything exist at all? Is it due to the existence of something necessary, like God? Or did something just have to be; or is it contingent that anything exists at all? Could nothing have existed?

Existence and Ontology: What does it mean for something to 'exist'? Do only physical things exist, or are there also non-physical 'abstract' things, like universals or mathematical objects? Do everyday objects exist 'independently' of our beliefs and perceptions, or are they mind-dependent?

Material composition: What is the nature of ordinary objects? Do they even exist, or do only collections of simples exist? The problem of material composition, i.e., Universalism, Nihilism, Organicism. This question also raises a methodological issue about metaphysics: is this a serious metaphysical dispute or 'just a verbal' dispute?

Teaching Methods:
In class: This course mixes lectures and in-class discussion (peer-to-peer and student-to-teacher) around metaphysical questions, arguments, and methodological questions surrounding how to approach or resolve long-standing questions in metaphysics. This means 2x two hours per week in class.

Reading prior to class: Each class is paired with one textbook reading and one article in metaphysics. You are expected to read these before attending class. Reading time (without note taking) corresponds to approx. 1 1/2 hour per class.

Attendance is mandatory (no more than two classes maximum unless there are exceptional circumstances).

Method of Assessment:
(1) Written in-class examination (70%).
(2) Reflection debate (write-share-pair: students write a short piece arguing for or against a position in metaphysics; then students share it with a classmate for critique as well as complement, where applicable) (30%).

Required literature:

Conee, E. and Sider, T. (2014). Riddles of Existence: A Guided Tour of Metaphysics. Oxford University Press.

Garrett, B. (2017). What is this thing called Metaphysics? Routledge.

Selected articles (see Canvas)

Course Objective:
After completing this course, you are able to:

identify and explain philosophical positions and concepts concerning the mind-body problem, distinguishing between dualism, identity theory, functionalism, computationalism, illusionism, and 4E approaches;

apply philosophical positions and concepts to case studies involving consciousness, free will, and mental disorders;

dissect philosophical arguments to examine their logical structure and underlying assumptions;

reflect on the implications of philosophical positions within scientific and social contexts;

develop and present your own view on a philosophical topic in written form.

Course Content:
The relationship between the mind and the body has puzzled philosophers for centuries, giving rise to the notorious mind–body problem. In this course, students will gain insight into a diverse range of philosophical positions proposed to address this problem, including substance dualism, property dualism, identity theory, functionalism, computationalism, and illusionism. We will examine the strengths, weaknesses, and implications of each perspective, shedding light on the complexity inherent in understanding the nature of the mind and its relation to the physical world. In addition to traditional approaches, the course will also explore embedded and extended approaches, which emphasize the importance of the environment for our mental lives. These discussions will address the special status of consciousness as well as emerging questions concerning interaction with technology and artificial intelligence. Finally, we will consider two key case studies central to the philosophy of mind. First, do we possess free will, or are our actions always predetermined? Second, what does it mean to be “mentally ill,” and how can we assess the “proper” functioning of the mind?

Learning Objectives

Understand and apply ethical theories: You have a basic understanding of the most important ethical systems and how they affect contemporary discussions on the impact of neurotechnologies.

Neuroscientific research and emerging neurotechnologies give rise to a range of social, legal, and ethical issues. These include potential threats to privacy, new forms of manipulation, the regulation of cognitive enhancement, brain-based predictions of human behavior, and questions surrounding free will and consciousness. In this course, you will become familiar with the most important concepts and positions in philosophical debates on these topics. This includes the mind–body problem and its influence on neuroscientific research, debates about consciousness and free will, the major ethical systems and their impact on contemporary discussions of neurotechnologies, the philosophical foundations of current debates on science, technology, and AI, as well as the moral and epistemological implications of algorithms for both individuals and society.

Knowledge and understanding:

Course Content:
Political philosophy or political theory (often used interchangeably) deals with hot topics in today’s society. Together we explore the ideas and visions that people use when designing, redesigning or assessing the way their society is organized. In this course you get to know the most important past and contemporary ideologies within the modern political spectrum, such as liberalism, socialism, feminism, ecological thinking. We also look - particularly during the lectures - at the historical-cultural background of these ideologies: where do they come from, what are the core ideas?

And we practice as well public debates, and reflecting on your own opinions, together with people from very different backgrounds. Listening is as important as talking. This is partly done in the lectures, partly in the university-wide Broader Mind Course, which is associated with this course.

We always try to do this in an informed, academic way: arguments are key. But in the selection of arguments political ideologies are important maps for people. In the past, from Plato, but certainly in modern times, all kinds of ideas and visions have been formed that inspire people and on which people rely on in dealing with issues in society.

The course has two parts. The main part will be offered in Period 1. Next to this you will participate, with your philosophical background acquired in Period 1, in the university-wide offered Broader Mind Course, which is organized in the spring (period 4 and 5, in total 40 hours), in which you will meet students from all faculties of the VU and together work on and discuss themes that focus on personal development and societal challenges (and the relations between those). In the main course, we will study poltical ideologies and apply these already to current societal issues as well as to some themes that will be discussed as well in the Broader Mind Course. What do the various political ideologies have to say on inequality, on climate change, on abortion rights, on drugs use, on education? You may self choose the topic that you want to explore and discuss. them. Discussions will take place as 'talkshows'.

Course Objective:
The goal of this course is to acquire insight into a classical text of the history of philosophy: Kant’s “Kritik der reinen Vernunft”. This text is treated on a textual level but also positioned in the perspective of a broader framework of the history of philosophy, in particular that of metaphysics and empiricism.

After this course,

you can explain basic concepts of Kant’s KrV in your own words;

you have obtained insight into the basic question of the KrV as well as in its argumentation and structure;

you can position Kant’s transcendental philosophy in the history of philosophy;

you can read and analyze texts of Kant by yourself;

you have developed more general academical skills like close reading of texts, discussing them critically, and writing about them.

Course Content:
In his "Kritik der reinen Vernunft" (1781/1787), the first of his three critical works, Kant developed his famous as well as infamous philosophical ‘Copernican turn’ with respect to our knowledge claims. The significance of the KrV for the history of philosophy can hardly be overestimated. Kant's conception of ‘transcendental philosophy’ aims to supply philosophy with a completely new foundation, namely a ‘critical’ foundation. According to Kant, both metaphysics and empiricism are uncritical regarding their own presupposition. Hence, Kant’s KrV not only establishes a new philosophical paradigm but at the same time positions this paradigm within the history of philosophy. For many philosophers, Kant’s transcendental philosophy showed to be a source, a standard, and of course an instance that is in need of criticism itself. The history of philosophy cannot be understood properly without knowledge of Kant’s philosophy. It seems that a philosophy that falls back behind to Kant’s position does not have a long future. In the course, we study in great detail the Einleitung of the KrV (= 2e editie, B 1-30), parts from the Transzendentale Ästhetik and the Transzendentale Logik (Analytik der Begriffe). We start with the Einleitung, following the order of the sections, and hence start with the first section. It is recommended to have read the whole Einleitung before the first meeting. At least, students are supposed to have prepared §§ 1-3 (B 1-10) for the first meeting. For the further meetings too, students have to prepare themselves by studying the relevant text.

Seminar, supplemented by lectures as a part of the seminar. Due to the fact that the goal of this course can only be achieved by means of an active interaction, attendance is mandatory: who misses more than 1 meeting cannot do an (re)examination.

The re-examination only consists of an open book test (grades for the assignments are not taken into account). (learning objectives 1-5)

Course Objective:
The Broader Mind Course is an extracurricular, interdisciplinary course focused on your personal development in relation to challenging societal issues. In small groups of bachelor students from diverse disciplines and VU faculties, you will meet in person to explore and discuss issues you may already be encountering in your life – or may face in your future career. You will practice and develop key social and academic skills essential for both personal and societal transformation; competencies that are highly valued in today’s workplace.

You will grow not only as a person, but also as both a citizen and an academic.

Among the skills that you will practice are:

Communication (public speaking, presenting your own opinion, active listening, debating).

Cooperation (working in interdisciplinary groups).

Problem solving and innovation (conflict resolution, challenging existing ideas, creating original solutions).

Ability to deal with complexity and ambiguity (self-introspection, empathy, perspective taking, mediation).

What is in it for you?

Earn a Certificate and Edubadge to boost your CV and personal leadership.

Sharpen your critical and creative thinking with real-world challenges.

Reflect on your beliefs and how they shape your worldview.

Listen to diverse perspectives and engage with disagreement constructively.

Explore new ways of thinking through dialogue, reflection and imagination.

Connect with curious minds and broaden your view of the world and yourself.

The course load can be easily combined with your regular study program as the work loads consists of about 2 hours of work per week on average, while it runs in periods 4 and 5 (except during exam and assessment weeks). All in all, very manageable, and all the more exciting given how impactful those 2 hours can be!

• Track A: Success & Failure, Poverty, Human Body, Rebellion
• Track B: Health & Happiness, Digital World, Viewpoints & Worldview, Sustainability

Step 2: Explore the Themes online and offline
