Course Objective:
Perhaps the best way to answer the question “What is this course going to be about?” is to predict what you are likely to learn in this term. As we engage the course materials, you will know, can reproduce knowledge, and have insight regarding:

Basic chronological and historical information about Buddhism—that is to say, about its ‘history’ in a factual sense.

The universe (‘cosmology’) of Buddhism, and thus Asia generally, its gods and spirits and powers.

The major movements of ideas and practices in Buddhism over time.

The major forces acting on Buddhism over time: political, economic, philosophical, practical, and so on.

The major sources for the study of Buddhism: texts, art and archaeology, secular sources, modern ethnography, etc. Naturally, we will not be able to cover all sources and disciplines equally well.

To accomplish these objectives, during the course, in its writing assignments and group discussions (1.1–5), you will typically be doing the following: you will actively and systematically reflect on and apply the acquired knowledge and insight, regarding:

The nature of Buddhist authority and its sources.

Regionalism and its effects.

The culture dynamics of the ‘emergence’ and so-called ‘spread’ of Buddhism in Asia and beyond.

The relation of non-modern forms of Buddhism to modernisation movements and Buddhist Modernism.

The culture dynamics and characteristics of so-called Global Buddhism.

By nature of the disciplinary backgrounds of the SRT School of Religion and Theology and in alignment with the Buddhist Seminary and our Spiritual Care trajectories that offer this course, its core, and starting point for our explorations, is not only concerned with introductory matter regarding the (social) history of Buddhist ideas and practices, but also their contemporary developments and application in professional fields, such as applied mindfulness techniques and the work of Buddhist caregivers. Those in the Religious Studies Spiritual Care track, besides Religious Studies theoretical frames, will also address professional and societal applications. You will evaluate and discuss:

What happens when Buddhism is framed in terms of ‘religion’, as an object of the discipline of Religious Studies?

The relation of Buddhist contemplative expertise and helping professions.

How traditional Buddhist goals are gradually finding their place in ever shifting late modern worldviews and self-understandings.

The place of Buddhism in life (yes, we shall also think BIG).

The tensions that are resolved or brought out by Buddhist thought and practices (just in case you hadn’t noticed …).

There will be no regional limitations, but our forays will have a natural, historical centre of gravity in the regions of origin, in what presently is India and Nepal. At each and every turn of our historical and doctrinal forays we shall also look into how things work: the basic concepts and operating premises of Buddhism: so, we’ll be dealing with both. We shall try to understand instances of Buddhism within history, not by moving strictly chronologically through that history but by contrasting selected cases with other cases. Our questions will both allow us to span historical periods and demand that we see things in comparative aspect. A sample of the kinds of questions we shall think about:

What is our human condition? What can we do about it? How can we assist others, professionally and otherwise?

In fact, what do we owe others? What do they owe us?

Who is in charge in all that? How is that decided, and by whom?

In fact, whose Buddhism are we talking about?

What is the fate of the dead? What can be done about it?

How can Buddhism and Buddhist-derived techniques such as mindfulness, loving kindness or compassion be applied in the helping professions?

Last but not least: self-reflexively, who are we that we are interested in Buddhism?

Course Content:
This course provides a general introduction to Buddhism, as so-called religious system, set of philosophies and doctrines, and cultural force. The course surveys the historical background of Buddhism from its Indian origins through its development and spread—eventually also outside ‘Asia’—by means of lectures, reading selected primary sources (in translation), secondary sources and, not least of all, by also way of group discussion. This course, at its broadest, should help you to at least begin to answer the question: “What is Buddhism?” I assume that since you are here, this is (one of) your question(s).

Yet, the study of Buddhism also provides an excellent opportunity to approach basic human questions of an entirely general type. So, it is possible that you find the philosophy of Buddhism attractive, perhaps as an alternative to some traditions with which you are familiar, or that you have another personal reason for your interest. Needless to say, these are all valid. The approach of the course is nonetheless entirely non-confessional, meaning that we aim to look as objectively as possible at Buddhism as an object of study. However, the fact that we ought to distinguish emic and etic perspectives carefully, doesn’t preclude switching between them wherever helpful—that would be very much encouraged, in fact.

In addition, some argue that there are more academic and less personal reasons to study Buddhism as well. For instance, that it is the only cultural force—in fact, the only reason other than sheer geography—that justifies speaking of something called “Asia” at all, for it is through Buddhism that Sri Lanka and Japan share a common vocabulary of cosmology, mythology, the ideal ruler, and much more.

Appraises and can explain how things appear “in the eye of the beholder”: i.e., appreciation of the reflection of our own history of religious ideas in the marriage of convenience between Buddhism and psychology, and recognition of our tendencies to ‘psychologise’ the sacred and to ‘sacralise’ psychology.

Demonstrates critical discernment regarding the problematic nature of patently modernist categories such as ‘immediate experience’ in modernist framings of Buddhism and the implied epistemic paradoxes.

Course Content:
Summary: Since the late nineteenth century, various forms of Buddhism emerged from modernising Asia and, with apparent ease, penetrated new cognitive, spiritual and cultural domains—many far removed from their origins, geographically as well as epistemically. In the process, Buddhism became abbreviated to ‘meditation’ and later even to mindfulness, and a curious marriage of convenience emerged between Buddhism and psychology. How did this come to pass and what does the most recent global rise of interest tell us about Buddhism, and what does it reveal about those who are interested?

In this course we shall also explore that fascinating marriage of convenience between Buddhism and psychology by tracing the reception history and mainstreaming of mindfulness ‘meditation’. Literary, ritual, social, but also perceived spiritual and philosophical aspects of Buddhist traditions will come into view, in an exercise in Buddhist hermeneutics that is self-reflexive. The focus is on older Buddhist and Theravāda sources, which, by their perceived remoteness, challenge our own world views and self-understandings. It thus resumes the self-reflexive exercise of studying various religious traditions in so-called World Religions, but by engaging the case study of the reception history of mindfulness. Participants in this course will also be granted the opportunity to attend an Applied Buddhist Mindfulness training.

Long read: Mostly outside Asia and Asian communities abroad, Buddhism has almost become synonymous with meditation. More often than not, Buddhism is framed as a ‘science of the mind’ or ‘non-modern psychology’—as if it were not a contradiction in terms, given that psychology is the very flagship of modernity. The common language of popular Buddhism thus mostly derives from pop psychology. This language and particular mode of understanding indeed has become a prominent characteristic of global Buddhist modernism.

So when and how did this hermeneutical practice arise? As you will have ample opportunity to discover on this course, these somewhat complex processes of framing have been going on for quite some time; in fact, almost since the very birth of psychology as a discipline. In the end, such preferred readings of Buddhism may reveal more about the receiving cultures and the rise of global modernity than they do about Buddhism in its ‘original’ Asian contexts. This is about our specific history with religion, as exemplified in the transition through the age of Enlightenment and the rise of modern disciplines of science, secularisation, processes of individuation, interiorisation of the psyche and the increasing, at times sheer dazzling self-reflexivity of modernity, and, of course, the concomitant history of reception of Buddhism.

First and foremost, this class is an introduction to Theravāda forms of meditation, based on ‘Buddhist classics’, but there is also plenty of room for the experiential side of things. In this seminar we shall also have opportunity to reflect on the reception history and psychological interpretation of Buddhism. Bravely conquering our neophyte trepidation, we will leap into the deepest waters from the very outset. Our main sources of information on Buddhism will be original texts in translation, rather than second- or third-hand information and digests. We will first study several typical examples of Buddhist texts and genres; ‘typical’ in the sense that they have contributed to the widely held assumption that Buddhism, au fond, is some kind of non-modern form of psychology. Don’t let the technical nature and at times hermetical appearance of the Buddhist reading materials discourage you; many of these texts indeed appear a far cry from the Buddhist literature that is specifically produced for ‘Western’ audiences and which many of those interested in Buddhism in this ‘New Age’ may be familiar with. This is a different cup of tea altogether, not rarely steeped by the sharpest minds, greatest philosophers and most erudite scholars of pre-modern Asia. Some of these were also reputed to be accomplished yogis; but that is not as self-evident as it may seem. In fact, the very problems we experience when reading, understanding and contextualising the materials are what fuel the subsequent discourse and our discussions in this seminar.

We shall be reading, in translation, complicated, knowledge-intensive materials that often are difficult to penetrate without extensive commentary, notably sources on mindfulness and the Abhidharma model of the mind, detailing various aspects of the mental domain, but always in relation to outside elements in the world, pertaining to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, cyclic existence and its extinction: i.e., final release of the same (and be warned, again, these encompass more than fits our idea of an internalised psyche). We shall thus familiarize ourselves with the intricacies of Buddhist theories of perception and an abundance of Buddhist scholastic classifications pertaining to the mental domain. Struggling with these at times gnomic texts, we shall learn a thing or two about Buddhist worldviews, self-understandings, and on Buddhist perspectives on our human potential

This course on Buddhism and Psychology thus provides a rare journey of self-discovery, touching the very core of modern self-understanding, across receiving cultures globally. A journey on which we critically examine everything we meet on our way, questioning modernist Buddhist assumptions, received wisdom of current Buddhist Studies discourse, and even some of the points of departure of this very course, and where needed fundamentally to revise or reframe them, if you dare ...

Course Content:
Building on the Greek I module, the course of Greek II offers students a more extensive foundation for the independent study of the language of the Greek New Testament and of Early Christian, Jewish-Greek, and Greco-Roman sources that will be studied later in the curriculum. Students learn Koinē Greek through class attendance, collaborative discussion of assignments, and self-study. A more advanced knowledge of morphology and, in particular, syntax will be acquired, in order to enable to understand, analyse, and translate complex texts in Koinē Greek independently. During this course, students will also learn to use a Greek-English dictionary. Furthermore, building on the knowledge of translation methods acquired in Greek I and the more advanced linguistic competence developed the Greek II, students will learn to analyse existing translations on the basis of the Greek New Testament. With these tools, students will be enabled to reflect on their own and others’ interpretation choices with an open intellectual attitude and develop a critical scholarly approach to the text of the New Testament. Finally, the course students will allow students to situate Koinē Greek within the broader development of the Greek language.

The course is taught in English, but the final examination is bilingual and may be taken in Dutch.

After finishing this course, the student:

has gained knowledge on the intellectual, psychological and practical aspects of Yoga;

is able to define Yoga, articulate the purpose of Yoga, analyze different perspectives to Yoga, and understand its importance in our life;

is able to understand the history of Yoga;

has acquired knowledge and understanding of the complex content, conceptual development and religious role and significance of yoga philosophy;

has acquired an analytical insight into the positioning of Yoga within the Hindu tradition and other Indian philosophical schools of thinking;

is able to develop their conceptualization of Ashtanga Yoga through Patanjali Yoga sutras tradition and further, will be able to apply it towards an individual's developmental purposes;

has acquired knowledge and understanding of how to apply yogic principles in the context of leadership and entrepreneurship;

is able to apply the gained knowledge and insight to trace personal intellectual and spiritual development. Further adopt moral leadership (among others in business);

Course Content:
Introduction - In the age of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, questions of identity and purpose are central. This course explores how yoga—as both a philosophy and a practice—can guide self-awareness and conscious leadership. Students engage with key yogic concepts and apply them to business and entrepreneurship, drawing from related Indic traditions that emphasize body–mind integration.

Background - Rapid technological change (AI, quantum computing, mixed reality) is transforming our world, often creating uncertainty and complexity (VUCA). Leaders today must navigate fast-paced, multicultural, and ethically diverse environments. This course positions yoga as a tool for developing inner clarity, resilience, and intercultural understanding in such contexts—skills vital for contemporary leadership and entrepreneurship.

General Aim - Yoga is more than a set of physical exercises; it offers a comprehensive worldview. Recognized globally for its value in personal and professional well-being, yoga is now practiced in many organizations. This course introduces yoga as a transformative path—philosophical and practical—linked to leadership, ethical business, and self-realization. It also examines parallels with mindfulness traditions and contemporary applications in decision-making and innovation.

Course Themes

Unit 1 – Yoga in the Hindu Worldview: Meaning, purpose, types (Jnana, Karma, Bhakti Yoga)

Unit 2 – Historical Development: From Vedas to the present

Unit 3 – Philosophical Perspectives: Yoga in the Gītā and Hatha Yoga texts

Unit 4 – Ashtanga Yoga: The eightfold path

Unit 5 – Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras: Key concepts, yogic mind theory, comparison with Western psychology

Unit 6 – Yoga at the Micro Level: Inner well-being, ethical and educational impact

Unit 7 – Yoga at the Macro Level: Coping with VUCA, integrative thinking

Unit 8 – Experiential Practice: Self-awareness, reflection, personal yogic diary

Teaching Methods:
The methodology used is a combination of reading texts, interpretation of text, videos, discussions and experiential practices. The course participants will do self-study, interact with each other, learn by practicing, demonstrate their understanding of concepts through assignments, presentations and a term paper.

This 7-week course consists of two interactive sessions per week, which students are strongly encouraged to attend fully for optimal personal and academic growth. All essential information and materials are shared via the Canvas page, and students are expected to complete the readings beforehand to actively engage in discussions and Q&A during class. Questions requiring deeper reflection should be posted on the Canvas discussion forum, where students are also encouraged to explore how course content relates to their personal or professional lives. Participants may be asked to present or discuss assigned readings, and will engage in both group discussions and basic yoga practices introduced during designated sessions.

Method of Assessment:
- Group Presentation (20%)
- Individual Term Paper (80%)

Knowledge, insight and communicating are tested in the end of term paper. Applying the practice in personal situations can also form part of the end of term paper but will also become visible through the presentations. Developing intellectual and psychological skills are tested through the presentations.

All AI-assisted work must be properly disclosed and remain the student’s own intellectual contribution. Undisclosed or excessive AI use may be considered plagiarism and handled accordingly.

Course Content:

Course Objective:
By the end of this course, students will:

Gain a solid understanding of how spirituality is approached in religious studies, especially through anthropological and sociological perspectives, and explore how scholarly approaches to spirituality have evolved in recent decades.

Examine the relationship between religion and spirituality, using Buddhism and mindfulness as key case studies, and engage with debates around spirituality as distinct from religion as well as theories that see spirituality as central to religious meaning.

Understand the historical and cultural processes that have shaped today’s ideas about spirituality, recognizing that many concepts often seen as timeless are, in fact, relatively recent and shaped by specific contexts.

Learn to distinguish between academic (etic) and insider (emic) perspectives on spiritual practices, exploring how these perspectives frame understandings of spirituality within particular cultural and historical settings.

Reflect on their own positionality and consider how personal background, assumptions, and experiences influence their interpretation of spiritual and religious practices.

Explore how spirituality intersects with key contemporary issues such as environmentalism, gender, the global spread of Asian religious practices (especially mindfulness), and the self-help movement.

Critically engage with media portrayals of spirituality — from films and TV shows to podcasts and documentaries — and analyze how these representations shape popular understandings and circulate globally.

Build academic skills in reading, analyzing, and discussing scholarly literature, preparing them to participate thoughtfully in discussions about the study of spirituality and its place in today’s world.

Course Content:
What’s behind the global buzz around “spirituality”? Is it a new form of religion, a tool for self-help, or a symptom of today’s neoliberal societies? This course explores recent shifts in the global religious landscape, focusing on the changing discourses of spirituality and its complex, often contested, relationship with religion.

We will examine how spirituality is approached in the academic study of religion, drawing on anthropological and sociological perspectives to trace its emergence as a modern concept shaped by historical, cultural, and political forces. Special attention will be given to the global rise of mindfulness, its Buddhist roots, and how it has been repackaged in self-help, healthcare, and corporate settings. Students will critically analyze how mindfulness intersects with neoliberalism, gender, commercialization, and cultural appropriation.

Another key theme is the increasing pairing of spirituality with environmentalism, or so-called “green religion.” We will explore whether such movements reflect genuine religious innovation or adaptations to today’s consumer-driven and ecologically fragile world.

Media representations—whether in films, TV shows, or documentaries—are central to how spiritual practices are understood and popularized. Students will investigate how these portrayals shape public perceptions and fuel the global spread of spiritual ideas.

Finally, the course invites students to reflect on their own positions as observers and participants, working with both insider (emic) and outsider (etic) perspectives. By combining theoretical analysis with attention to practical applications, students will gain a nuanced understanding of the diverse ways spirituality is practiced, interpreted, and represented in today’s world.

Teaching Methods:
The course combines short lectures, focused discussions, group work, and engagement with media such as movies, TV shows, podcasts, and documentaries, both in class and at home.

Course Objective:
After finishing this course, the student is able to:

understand and apply with confidence key concepts from the study of religion and gender, such as: agency,hermeneutics of suspicion, embodiment, intersectionality;

describe important shifts in the study of religion and gender, such as the post-secular turn, the corporeal turn, the postcolonial turn, queering religion

describe analytically how gender and sexuality have been regulated within religions, as well as how in secularised societies, gender is used to regulate the presence of religion in the public sphere;

articulate major parallels and differences between a number of religious traditions in their approaches to gender issues in the past and present;

describe both religious insider views and academic outsider views;

link present-day debates and phenomena to historical patterns.

Course Content:
Within feminist movements and studies, religion and gender equality have often been seen as opposing, perhaps even mutually exclusive categories. Institutionalized religion has been identified as one of the main actors in the oppression of women and LGBTIQ+ people. And indeed, religion in past and present has formulated a gendered ethics that has at times resulted in gender inequality, to say the least. As a result, in Western contexts in particular, the emancipation of gendered and sexual minorities has automatically been linked to the process of secularization. At the same time, the academic disciplines of religious studies and theology have not always been open to incorporate feminist, queer and trans perspectives.

Over the past few decades, however, the study of religion and gender, as well as queer and trans perspectives on religion, have been flourishing. Scholars have increasingly become aware of the fact that the majority of women (cis and trans) as well as LGBTIQ+ people either identify as religious, have been brought up as believers, or live in a country where the majority of the population are religious. Moreover, it has been pointed out that secularism has not necessarily been beneficial to women and sexual minorities, either. And, finally, scholars have become more attuned to the fact that the emancipation of women and LGBTIQ+ people has been misused in nationalistic rhetoric in order to discredit and ‘other’ religious groups, most notably Muslims.

This course maps significant developments in the study of religion and gender, as well as related fields such as that of queer and trans studies of religion. By discussing central themes, and by approaching these from both contemporary as well as historical perspectives, the course shows how contemporary debates are rooted in historical formations of religious narratives. Examples include contemporary and past religions (Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and ancient Greek religion).

Course Content:

Course Objective:
After finishing this course, the student

has professional knowledge in the field of key Biblical texts about Peace and Justice, and is able to analyze them and to interpret them independently;

is able to do literature research in the field of historical background and literary context of these Biblical texts, and is able to apply the results for a deeper understanding of the Bibli cal texts;

has professional knowledge in the field of Biblical texts that contain warfare and violence and is able to analyze them from theological and ethical perspectives;

is able to articulate the Biblical/theological concepts of peace and justice in his/her own words. He/she is able to explain their relevance for ethics (and theology) in the world today, also to members of non christian religions and to secular people;

is able to deal in a constructive and responsible manner with questions about war and violence in the Bible, and is able to articulate his/her own position on this subject and to lead a dialogue with representatives of other positions;

is able to relate the concepts of justice and peace to relevant themes and conflicts in present-day society, and is is able to reflect on her/his own postion and to relate it to other religious and secular positions.

Course Content:
Students will analyze texts which allow for elaboration on the meaning of ‘peace’ and ‘justice’ in biblical texts: examples include the Sermon on the Mount; key verses form the Gospel of Luke; visions of peace and critiques of social injustice in prophetic books; and key texts from the Psalms and the Torah. Several questions will be considered in relation to these texts. How are the concepts of peace and justice interconnected within the Bible? What is the relationship between divine and human justice?
Students will also study texts on the so-called ‘Holy War’; narratives about the cycle of violence in human lives; verses that portray God acting violent; and prayers for God’s revenge on enemies. Their function in context will be discussed, and important questions will come to the fore. The violent content notwithstanding, which texts provide a constructive and justice-supporting message? How should Biblical texts which do not support peace be dealt with?
Finally, students will discuss questions of application, for example:
Which modern ethical and theological concepts of peace and justice answer to a Biblical perspective on peace and justice?

Course Objective:
After finishing this course, the student

has studied and compared different types of fundamentalism and fundamentalist movements;

has examined the complex relation of fundamentalism with related phenomena, such as nationalism, extremism, radicalisation, and (terrorist or extremist) violence;

is able to recognize the methodological differences in the multidisciplinary field of fundamentalism studies;

is able to recognize various approaches to explain fundamentalism;

is able to critically reflect on the concept ‘fundamentalism’, the different ways to conceptualize and define it, and the aptness of the concept;

has improved critical reading, presentation, and writing skills.

Course Content:
Fundamentalism manifests itself in numerous contemporary political and social movements that demonise and harm others and can even pose a threat to democracy: White Christian Nationalism (in Russia, the US, etc.), End Times Fascism/ extremist transhumanism, ISIS, right-wing extremism (e.g. the German AfD), the ideology of Hamas, nationalist-extremist Zionism, and so on.

Since the beginning of fundamentalist movements in the early 20th century, public and academic discourse has viewed fundamentalism as harmful to our societies. It is seen as reactionary, anti-democratic, anti-pluralistic, anti-scientific, and militant. Much research has focussed on violent forms of fundamentalism, and has associated the phenomenon with violent extremism and terrorism. In spite of this negative verdict on fundamentalism, it is far from clear what the term ‘fundamentalism’ actually means. Nor is it clear how it relates to phenomena such as nationalism, extremism, radicalisation, and (terrorist or extremist) violence, how to best explain why fundamentalism occurs, or how to engage with fundamentalists.

The course starts by scrutinising various definitions and conceptualisations of ‘fundamentalism.’ It then zooms in on fundamentalist movements from the Christian, Jewish and Islamic traditions, and considers Hindu and Buddhist variants of fundamentalism. In due course, the complex relation between fundamentalism and nationalism will be scrutinised. We will then turn to the question how to explain fundamentalism, and what we mean by ‘explaining’ such a phenomenon. Moreover, we will reflect on the question how fundamentalism relates to adjacent phenomena such as radicalisation, extremism, and terrorism. The course concludes by addressing epistemological and ethical questions regarding fundamentalism: what is the role of indoctrination, education, or echo chambers for fundamentalist convictions, and how should we engage with fundamentalists?

Course Objective:
General aim - This course enables students to critically explore how spiritual worldviews, particularly from Hindu traditions, contribute to sustainability thinking, and to examine how spirituality informs personal values and collective responsibility.

Learning goals - By the end of this course, students are able to:

Explain foundational concepts of spirituality, self, and mind in Hindu traditions and relate them to contemporary sustainability challenges.

Compare and contextualise Hindu philosophical insights with Western perspectives on reality, human nature, and ecological responsibility.

Interpret Hindu approaches to sustainability in relation to technological and societal disruption, and the increasing complexity and uncertainty of our global future.

Apply insights from Hindu spiritual traditions to reflect on one’s own values, worldview, and personal development in relation to sustainability.

Assess and reflect critically on alternative paradigms and spiritual approaches to well-being at individual and societal levels.

Demonstrate academic skills—including intellectual curiosity, critical thinking, and academic self-confidence—relevant to the study of Hindu worldviews.

Communicate newly acquired insights clearly and coherently in both academic writing and oral presentations, using appropriate terminology and argumentation.

Course Content:
This course explores how the Hindu worldview, with its emphasis on the sacredness of nature and spiritual ecology, offers valuable insights into sustainability and well-being. Drawing on key Hindu texts and traditions—especially from Vedānta, the Upaniṣads, and the Bhagavad Gītā—participants examine concepts of self, mind, and nature in relation to contemporary challenges such as climate change, technological disruption, and VUCA conditions. Through reflection and practical engagement, students will critically assess how spirituality can shape sustainable thinking at both individual and societal levels, including applications within the Green Economy.

Course themes: This course covers six thematic units:

Spirituality & Sustainability – Definitions, dimensions, and ethical relevance for personal, social, and ecological well-being.

Mind, Self & Consciousness – Hindu psychological views on mindset, self-awareness, and their impact on sustainability.

Interconnectedness – Spiritual practices fostering connection with nature and community; case studies on sustainable living.

Worldviews & Dharma – Hindu values and the SDGs; applying spiritual principles to global equity and environmental challenges.

VUCA & Disruption – Navigating global complexity using Hindu insights; paradigm shifts from ego-centric to integrative thinking.

Spirituality in Work & Society – Purpose-driven leadership, ethical business, and aligning inner development with societal change.

Teaching Methods:
Methodology - This course uses an active, student-centered approach that integrates academic insight with personal reflection. Learning takes place through interactive seminars, case-based and experiential activities (e.g. simulations), flip-classroom presentations, reflective writing, and group dialogue. Students conduct independent research culminating in a final paper that blends scholarly analysis with personal perspective, supported by peer and instructor feedback. They are also invited to co-design elements of the reflective work and focus areas. This approach fosters ownership, critical thinking, and deeper understanding of how spiritual worldviews relate to sustainability challenges.

Method of Assessment:
Assessment - The course assessment consists of four components:

Term Paper (50%) - A final academic paper in which students explore a self-chosen topic connecting Hindu spirituality with sustainability. The paper must demonstrate academic research, integration of course concepts and models, critical reflection, and personal insight.

Class Assignments (20%) - Four written or experiential assignments based on course activities. These assess understanding and application of key ideas, critical thinking, and the ability to connect theory to practice in creative ways.

Flip Learning Assignment 1 (15%) - An individual presentation interpreting Hindu texts through ecological and ethical lenses. Students demonstrate comprehension, argumentative clarity, and relevance to SDGs and course literature.

Flip Learning Assignment 2 (15%) - An individual or paired presentation on organizational spirituality and sustainability strategies. Students reflect on real-world cases, apply course models and CSR frameworks, and present well-reasoned insights.

In line with VU’s academic integrity policy, students may use AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Grammarly) for ideation and language refinement, but not for generating full assignments or reflective content. All AI-assisted work must be properly disclosed and remain the student’s own intellectual contribution. Undisclosed or excessive AI use may be considered plagiarism and handled accordingly.

Course Objective:
Upon completion of the course, students can:

Denote the visual and imaginative instruments for revealing, producing and transmitting sacred and divine realities and experiences in and through religion and film.

Is able to reflect critically on the practice of interpretation in film, especially in relation to religious themes and representations.

Has insight into how religious assumptions shape the depiction of religion and the sacred in film.

Understands that interpreting religious elements in film differs from interpreting secular content, especially given the symbolic and affective power of religious imagery.

Is able to apply different interpretive methods (e.g. symbolic, narrative, postcolonial, theological) to analyze religious themes in film.

Describe and apply a ‘film as religion’ approach to film, with a specific focus on the dimensions of myth, ritual, morality, transcendence and sacredness.

Can explain how filmmakers apply visual tools to deal with ‘the real’ and ‘the unspeakable’ and the limits of articulation and representation.

Course Content:
This course explores the limits of truth-telling and representation. Semantic and text-based approaches have a limited capacity to express the lived experience of people. This is perhaps most obvious when it comes to individual or collective trauma; to the void of reality that is beyond expression (the ‘real’ in Lacanian thinking); and to the experienced presence of sacred and divine realities - three experiences that are often referred to as the ‘unspeakable’, as something beyond articulation. In comparison to purely verbal representations of such experiences, film offers a rich repertoire of audiovisual tools that offers many opportunities of representing realities that are difficult to express in language. In this course, such filmic representations are explored by analyzing the cinematographic and narrative elements of film. In addition, the course discusses the limits of filmic representation as well, for film has its limits too when it comes to traumatic and sacred experiences: they can be not only unspeakable, but also ‘unimaginable’. However, film can at the very least probe the boundaries of what can be expressed; filmic methods and techniques can be mobilized to show what it means not to be able to imagine, not to be able to speak. In the third place, this course not only explores the representation of the ‘unspeakable’; it also applies a film as religion approach that enables students to understand the ‘religious work’ of film: how film may mediate (reveal, produce and transmit) sacred and divine realities and experiences. Students learn to unravel the representation and mediation of the unspeakable by carefully analyzing the cinematographic and narrative elements of film.

Course Objective:
General aim

The course aims to provide participants with a foundational understanding of key Hindu texts and traditions, including their religious, philosophical, cultural, and spiritual significance. Participants will gain an appreciation for the complexity and diversity of Hindu textual traditions, the importance of Sanskrit, and the role of Hindu epistemology and hermeneutics in understanding spiritual transformation. In response to the changing reality of generative and agentic AI, the course also aims to prepare students to become critically competent readers of AI-mediated textual evidence. Students will learn not merely to use AI tools, but to examine how knowledge is transformed when texts become datasets, prompts, embeddings, summaries, and machine-generated interpretations. They will also learn why query-based and text-grounded methods remain essential for responsible scholarship, since such methods require researchers to define what counts as evidence and to test interpretive claims against the text.

Learning goals - By the end of the course, participants will be able to:

Define key terms and concepts related to Hindu texts and traditions, including Śruti, Smṛti, Śāstra, Saṃhitā, pramāṇa, dharma, ātmā, jñāna, mokṣa, and puruṣārtha.

Understand the philosophical background of Hinduism, including Hindu worldview, ontology, epistemology, and the knowledge trinity of knowable, knowledge, and knower.

Identify and analyze major categories of Hindu texts, including Vedas, Vedāṅgas, Upaniṣads, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, Kāvya, Darśanas, Śāstras, and Saṃhitās.

Analyze selected themes from Hindu scriptures and traditions with attention to Sanskrit terminology, textual genre, commentary traditions, philosophical context, and lived spiritual practice.

Develop critical awareness of Sanskrit and non-translatables, recognizing how terms such as dharma, ātmā, Īśvara, jñāna, śraddhā, bhakti, and mokṣa may be distorted when reduced to approximate English equivalents.

Understand the relevance of Hindu texts and traditions for Indian culture, philosophy, spirituality, ethics, society, and contemporary life.

Approach indigenous research through Hindu worldviews, with attention to researcher preparation, embodied knowing, epistemic humility, and the role of the knower in the production of knowledge.

Become critically competent readers of AI-mediated textual evidence, able to evaluate AI-generated interpretations of Hindu texts by asking what the source is, what textual evidence is being used, what Sanskrit terms are being flattened, which interpretive tradition is assumed, and what the AI may have omitted or hallucinated.

Evaluate whether and how AI can be understood within a Hindu epistemological framework, especially in relation to pramāṇa, śabda, anumāna, satya, valid cognition, error, and hermeneutical responsibility.

Understand how knowledge changes when Hindu texts become digital objects such as datasets, prompts, embeddings, metadata, machine-generated summaries, searchable corpora, and AI-generated interpretations.

Distinguish between AI-assisted hypothesis generation and text-grounded evidence, recognizing that AI may help generate questions, compare perspectives, and summarize debates, but that scholarly claims must be checked against primary texts, commentaries, Sanskrit grammar, and accountable evidence.

Recognize query-based research as a discipline of intellectual honesty because it requires the researcher to define what counts as evidence, specify search criteria, make assumptions visible, and allow others to inspect or reproduce the research process.

Develop responsible digital-hermeneutical skills for Hindu textual study by comparing manual reading, traditional commentary, digital search, query-based exploration, and AI-generated interpretation.

Communicate their understanding of Hindu texts, traditions, spiritual transformation, and AI-mediated interpretation through academic writing, presentations, group work, and reflective analysis.

Course Content:
This course introduces key texts, concepts, and traditions of Hindu knowledge systems, with attention to spiritual transformation, Hindu epistemology, Sanskrit hermeneutics, and the changing reality of generative and agentic AI.

Unit 1: Hindu Epistemology – Foundations of the Hindu worldview, key philosophical categories, and the knowledge triad: knower, knowledge, and known. The unit also introduces distinctions between information, knowledge, wisdom, and spiritual transformation in the age of generative AI.

Unit 2: Knowledge, Texts, and Pramāṇa – Ways of knowing, organization of Śruti and Smṛti texts, oral traditions, and Hindu hermeneutics. This unit also examines whether and how AI-generated interpretations can be evaluated through pramāṇa theory, including questions of valid knowledge, hallucination, testimony, and textual evidence.

Unit 3: The Knower – Embodied knowing, researcher preparation, epistemic humility, the importance of non-translatables such as ātman, dharma, and Īśvara, and basic Saṃskṛta literacy relevant to textual engagement. The unit also considers the role of the knower as prompt-maker, evaluator, interpreter, and accountable scholar in AI-mediated interpretation.

Unit 4: Vedas and Vedāṅgas – Overview of the four Vedas, their associated literature such as Brāhmaṇas and Upaniṣads, ritual practices, and the six Vedāṅgas, including phonetics, grammar, etymology, meter, ritual timing, and related disciplines. The unit also explores digital preservation of Vedic texts, oral traditions, recitation, phonetics, metadata, and the relevance of Vedāṅga disciplines for AI-assisted Sanskrit and Vedic textual analysis.

Unit 5: Itihāsa and Purāṇas – Themes and teachings from the Rāmāyaṇa, Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha, Mahābhārata, Bhagavad Gītā, and key Purāṇas. The unit examines their role in shaping Hindu worldviews and contemporary relevance, while also considering AI-assisted comparison of translations and the limits of machine-generated summaries in interpreting narrative, dharma, bhakti, karma, and spiritual transformation.

Unit 6: Darśanas and Kāvya – Introduction to the six classical philosophical systems and major genres of Saṃskṛta literature, including epics, poetry, and drama, with attention to aesthetics, ethics, logic, debate, and cultural critique. This unit also introduces query-based exploration of recurring concepts, metaphors, and interpretive patterns, and examines how knowledge changes when Śāstra becomes a dataset through corpus methods and agentic AI.

Unit 7: Other Śāstras and Saṃhitās – Exploration of Dharmaśāstra, Arthaśāstra, Āyurveda, Śilpa Śāstra, and Nāṭya Śāstra, highlighting their relevance to law, politics, medicine, arts, and performance in historical and modern contexts. The unit also addresses AI, cultural heritage, responsible representation of Hindu knowledge systems, and ethical issues in digitizing, summarizing, and automating sacred and traditional knowledge.

Teaching Methods:
Methodology - The course will use a blended approach to learning, consisting of synchronous and asynchronous elements. It will include a combination of lectures, discussions, group activities, debates, reading texts, interpretation of text, case studies, reflective writing assignments and experiential practices. Participants will be encouraged to engage in critical thinking, analysis, and reflection in order to develop a deeper understanding of Hindu texts and traditions. They are expected to do self-study, participate actively in class discussions, contribute to group activities, demonstrate their understanding of concepts through presentations and a term paper.

Method of Assessment:
Assessment

Flip-learning classroom presentation or reflective write-up — 20% - In the flip-learning classroom presentation, participants demonstrate reflective insight into specific aspects of Hindu texts and traditions. Students may also choose to present a critical comparison between a primary Hindu text and a traditional commentary, two translations of a Sanskrit term or passage, a manual interpretation and an AI-generated interpretation, a textual claim and the evidence used to support it, or a Hindu epistemological concept and its relevance for evaluating AI-mediated knowledge.

Term paper — 80% - The term paper should discuss a subject of personal interest to the participant and include independent research using libraries, online academic resources, primary texts, commentaries, and, where appropriate, digital tools. In the paper, participants should demonstrate academic writing skills and the ability to investigate a particular aspect of Hindu texts and traditions in depth. Where students use AI tools, they must disclose how they used them and critically evaluate any AI-generated content rather than treating it as an authority. Students are encouraged to distinguish between AI-assisted hypothesis generation and text-grounded evidence. The paper should remain within 3000 to 4000 words. The term paper should include a short AI / Digital Evidence Reflection Appendix of 300–500 words, in which students briefly explain whether AI tools were used, what prompts or search methods were used, what was accepted, rejected, or revised, what primary textual evidence supports the final argument, and how Sanskrit terms or translations were checked.

Use of AI Tools

In line with VU’s academic integrity policy, students may use AI tools for brainstorming, developing preliminary questions, comparing interpretations, and improving language. AI tools may not be used to generate full assignments or replace the student’s own reflection, analysis, or textual engagement. Any use of AI must be disclosed. Students remain responsible for critically evaluating AI-generated claims, checking them against primary texts, scholarly literature, and relevant Sanskrit terminology. AI-generated output should not be treated as authoritative evidence. Undisclosed or excessive AI use may be considered plagiarism. In this course, AI is treated not only as a tool, but also as a contemporary challenge to epistemology and hermeneutics, especially when texts become datasets, prompts, summaries, and machine-generated interpretations.

Unit 5: Philosophical Unity - Exploration of theoretical and practical unity among the Darśanas and their integrative potential.

Unit 6: Contemporary Reflections - Application of Darśanic thought to modern issues such as social cohesion and personal growth through self-awareness.

have developed insights in the modern history and contemporary lived practice of one of the world’s most widespread and influential Buddhist traditions, with case studies spanning East and Southeast Asia, Europe, and North America.

Course Content:
What happens when ancient Buddhist teachings meet modern life? How do religious traditions adapt in the face of migration, secularization, and global change? This course explores these questions through the lens of one of the world’s most influential yet often overlooked Buddhist traditions: Mahayana Buddhism as practiced in China, Taiwan, Southeast Asia, and increasingly around the globe, including, as we will discover, right here in Amsterdam.

While rooted in the historical development of Buddhism in East Asia, the course places strong emphasis on how this tradition is lived today—in temples, homes, online spaces, and multicultural societies. Using a multidisciplinary approach that draws on history, anthropology, and sociology, students will explore themes such as the role of monastics and laypeople, ritual practices, gender and sexuality, ethical eating, and the entanglement of Buddhism with politics and social movements.

Far from being a static tradition, contemporary Chinese Buddhism offers a fascinating case study of how religions transform in response to modernity, migration, and globalization. Students will have the opportunity to engage directly with local practice through a fieldwork component at a Buddhist temple in the Netherlands, gaining firsthand insight into how global Buddhism is reimagined in European contexts.

This course is perfect for students eager to explore not only Buddhism but also the dynamic relationship between religion and society in the context of modernity and globalization. It’s an exciting opportunity to dive into the complexities of religious life in today’s rapidly changing world—no background in Chinese studies required!

This course combines lectures, discussions, and group presentations, where students will develop the ability to select a research theme, build a solid bibliography, and formulate a focused research question. You will gain practical experience in collecting, organizing, and analyzing academic texts to support your research projects.

An immersive fieldwork excursion to a Buddhist temple will provide valuable insight into Buddhist practices in a local context, while online materials will complement in-class learning.

Active participation is essential. To fully benefit from the course, students are expected to attend at least 80% of classes and prepare all assigned readings.

Method of Assessment:
Bibliography (15%): A well-organized list of academic sources relevant to your research topic, developed in consultation with the instructor. You will also demonstrate an understanding of how to build an academic bibliography while identifying at least one relevant disciplinary perspective (e.g., history, sociology, anthropology, or philosophy) to support your research.

Written Academic Literature Overview (50%): A critical summary of the existing academic literature on your chosen topic, leading to the formulation of a research question. This will evaluate your ability to engage with sources and incorporate them effectively into your research.

Group Presentation (15%): A collaborative presentation where your group presents findings, connecting them to the research question. This will assess your ability to communicate research effectively and work collaboratively.

Participation and Attendance (20%): Completion of all required readings, active participation in class discussions, and attendance of at least 80% of sessions. This ensures ongoing engagement with the course material throughout the term.

has an overview of medieval ideas on the unity between civic and ecclesiastical community;

has an overview of the ways in which the Anabaptist ecclesiastical model challenged these ideas on unity;

has an overview of early-modern debates on coexistence and toleration and the contribution the radical reformation made to these debates;

Course Content:
After the reformation had broken the unity of the western church, Europeans had to rethink ideas on unity, relationship between church and state, and the role of the church within the civic community. Dissenters made a significant contribution to the development of new modes of coexistence and to the development of ideas on religious toleration. Their presence as such challenged medieval ideas on unity; their view on the history of the western church called into question the close cooperation between church and state. Dissenters had many reasons to advocate for religious toleration. In their pleas for toleration the dissenters relied on social, political, economic and religious arguments. This course offers an overview of the early modern debates on religious coexistence and toleration and the contribution the radical reformation made to these debates.

Seminars. Students are expected to prepare two oral presentations on an early modern texts. Enhancing cultural diversity, students will be encouraged to read texts from different contexts and in different languages.

Have an overview of English-language Mennonite and Anabaptist theologies since the mid-20th century

Course Content:
Modern Anabaptist Theology: Being Church in the World

This class will introduce students to (English-language) Anabaptist/Mennonite theologies since the mid-20th century and the way they have understood the relation between the “church” and the “world.” Prominently, Anabaptist/Mennonite theologians have argued that the church should be distinct from the world, to which it is to witness God’s desire of peace. The church is thus understood as a “colony of heaven” or an “outpost” of the Kingdom of God.

In making this claim, theologians are inspired by (a particular interpretation of) Anabaptist history. Yet, as we will discover in this class, Anabaptist/Mennonite thinking has always been more plural than such constructive approaches allow for.

In recent times, the normative status of several influential Anabaptist and Mennonite theologians is being challenged for historical, political, theological and ethical reasons. Feminist and postcolonial critiques, as well as the changing character of the global church, contribute to the widening of Anabaptist/Mennonite theological interpretation.

Anabaptist and Mennonite theologies is today better imagined as a broad collection of conversations with a range of different approaches to the church, ethical/political issues, and the outside world. In this class, students will learn to assess that conversation and take their place within it.

Teaching Methods:
Each class meeting will combine lecturing and seminar discussions. The classes will be structured around lectures and group discussions of the assigned primary and secondary source readings from the textbooks. Attendance and participation in class is required.

Method of Assessment:
Students will take turns in presenting a (critical) summary of the chapter read for that class and 2-3 discussion questions. (30%)

Course Objective:
After this course, the student will

Have an overview of key theological, philosophical, and ecclesial approaches to freedom, community, and difference in the Christian and specifically Mennonite/vrijzinnig traditions

Be able to analyze how freedom, community, and difference interact in concrete church practices in historical and contemporary cases

Course Content:
How do we live together in difference? In recent times, this question seems to become increasingly fraught in our societies. It is also a question that has animated lively debate in religious communities such as that of the Anabaptists and Mennonites. While some have sought conformity in the church, others (in the vrijzinnig) tradition have embraced an individual freedom from dogmatic ties. Yet is individual freedom enough to tie a community together across differences?

In this class, we will ask how we can understand the relation between different notions of freedom, difference, and community, both within the church itself and in the church’s interaction with wider society. Particular attention will be given to the Anabaptist/Mennonite religious tradition and the resources it brings (both historical and contemporary) to approaching these questions. Finally, students will be acquainted with (and practically exercise) kinds of communication and facilitation that allow a shared life in difference and relation to take shape.

has acquired basic knowledge of and structural insight in global religions (Buddhism, Christianity, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism). Aim: religious literacy (historical, empirical).

has acquired analytical knowledge of similarities and differences between the ways in which these global religions have developed historically, in particular during the Axial Age and Modernity. Aim: historical comparison (systematic, precondition of interreligious dialogue).

is capable of presenting both insider and outsider views, among different religious views, and back and forth from academic views to religious views. Aims: empathy and theory (precondition of hermeneutics and diversity).

Course Content:
This course focuses on the acquisition of basic knowledge and analytical understanding of religion in general and of six transnational and transcultural religions (so-called ‘world religions’) in particular: Buddhism, Christianity, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism. The course offers basic access and in-depth insight into these religions and worldviews. Functioning as the introductory backbone course of religious literacy for several bachelor and minor programs in Religious Studies, it will go beyond a superficial overview.

Each religious tradition or worldview may be studied separately, as handbook chapters tend to do, but things become more interesting and relevant if such traditions and worldviews are also compared in terms of shared issues and patterns. The competence to compare is a much needed skill since people increasingly have to communicate across cultural and religious boundaries, in case of intercultural and interreligious dialogue in a context of global exchange.

In order to allow for structural comparisons between these global religions, their historical development will be traced. The historical perspective will draw from the Axial Age framework, on the one hand, and the Modernity framework, on the other hand. The Axial Age constituted a period of comparable cultural breakthroughs when the main ‘world religions’ emerged (around 550 BCE – 100 CE). Modernity is much later (1500 EC in Western Europe and 1800 EC in colonized parts of the non-Western world). Contemporary issues will be addressed against the background of the transition from traditional to modern forms of religion and in light of the ways in which these religions have come to cope with Modernity. A separate session will be dedicated to the definitions of 'religion' and to the notion of 'world religions.'

The academic field of Religious Studies starts from outsider views of religion that draw from theories of religion current in the Humanities and Social Sciences. But it also tries to take seriously how religious believers view and experience the world and their own traditions from within and the religious traditions of others from without. Thus, it includes the scholarly capacity of empathy to switch from outsider views to insider views and back again.

Course Objective:
After finishing this course, the student:

has acquired knowledge of myths worldwide and detailed knowledge of some well-known myths (and fairy tales) in particular;

has acquired insight into the shared functions of rituals and myths;

has acquired insight into the academic debate in myth and ritual studies and can apply some mythographic approaches to specific myths;

is able to compare myths worldwide within the respective frameworks offered by each of the classical schools of myth interpretation.

Course Content:
Cultures worldwide transmit stories about the origin of the cosmos at large, of humankind, of specific customs and institutions, of natural phenomena, of evil and suffering, stories about the problems involved in growing up and living together. These stories are felt to be meaningful beyond just entertaining their audience, if these stories are considered to express how things are deep down at any time, how things are basically meant to be. Myths express how things are fundamentally intertwined with the community that experiences these stories as of crucial value to their own way of life and identity. Myths are binding stories even to the point of the community ritualizing the form in which they are told and performed.

The puzzling thing for scholars is that across cultures, narrative motifs and plots in myths, legends, and fairy tales, but also social and psychological functions of myths seem strikingly similar, that is to say, sometimes and somehow but not all the time and not everywhere, and it is very hard to pin down when and where exactly. The same thing can be said of rituals. Why do people all over the world perform rituals? Does ritual behavior have the same functions everywhere and all the time? What are the links between myth and ritual? Do myths, legends, fairy tales, and rituals perform the same functions?

The main focus of this course will be on the classical interpretations of myths and fairy tales but attention will also be paid to the scholarly understanding of ritual and how myth and ritual are related.

One mythographic school of interpretation approaches ritual as the enactment of mythical stories, an approach that is contested by scholars who consider ritual as a type of behaviour that is done for its own sake, not primarily for storytelling. Narrative theories analyse the structure of plot patterns in terms of problem solving heroes with a quest who overcome challenges and reach heroic goals. Other schools of interpretation apply Freudian or Jungian psychoanalysis. Structuralist theories also look for underlying patterns in the arrangement of narrative motifs but primarily along nature-culture lines. Classical and Renaissance philosophies embraced allegorical interpretations, whereas contemporary approaches stress the ideological function of myth and ritual in society and politics, in particular legitimizing power relations and nationalist inventions of tradition.

This course begins with the question 'Who are Jews?', exploring the remarkable diversity of the Jewish world across time and geography. Rather than approaching Judaism primarily as a historical subject, the course centers on Jewish texts, traditions, and lived practices, using history as background to illuminate the present.

Course Objective:
After finishing this course, the student:

has knowledge on different moral theories

has knowledge of different moral theories in religion and the way they are embedded in the religious (world)views

is (better) able to understand concrete moral problems in light of different ethical theories;

has heightened moral sensitivities;

has learnt that the perception of ethical issues is (to some extent) dependent upon cultural, religious and related presuppositions and that it is conceivable that there is more than one morally acceptable position;

has learnt to reflect critically on his/her own moral sentiments

has learnt that moral decision-making is a complex process that defies easy and straightforward solutions and that therefore reflecting seriously on moral issues is absolutely necessary (and that it is also fun!).

Course Content:
The aim of this course is to deepen the ability to reflect on moral issues in a responsible fashion. It focusses on moral theorizing in both philosophy and theology. The theorizing is supposed to guide the student’s abilities for critical reflection and enhance his/her capacity to analyze moral arguments from a philosophical as well as a theological viewpoint.

Issues that will be discussed are, among others, the following:

Moral Relativism/moral pluralism/moral absolutism: This is the issue as to whether there is one true (or adequate) morality, whether there are several adequate ones or an endless amount of adequate moralities (‘anything goes’). Relativists suggest that there are no trans-cultural criteria with the help of which we can justify moral considerations, thus, that ‘anything goes’ in morality. Moral absolutists suggest that there is exactly one true or adequate morality, usually the one they or their group hold. Moral pluralists are somewhere in the middle between both (they suggest that more than one morality can be adequate but that that does not imply that ‘anything goes’, i.e. not all kinds of moralities are adequate).

Possible case: How does e.g. the notion of human rights fare in light of those considerations? Does it require a morally absolutistic background rather than a relativist one? Can it be justified on pluralist grounds as well?

Utilitarianism versus Kantianism: This is the question whether our most basic moral criteria should be moral principles, such as ‘human beings should always be treated as an end in themselves and not as means to an end’. Should one make one’s actions only dependent on those principles (as some Kantians suggest?). Or should one take into account the consequences one’s actions have? For example, utilitarians suggest that we should take the consequences into consideration so as to maximize ‘the greatest happiness for the greatest number (of people)”.

Possible example: Depending on what kind of ethical approach one embraces, Kantian or utilitarian, one will look very differently at e.g. the practice of some NGO’s to pick up refugees in the Mediterranean Sea and take them to Europe. Those different approaches will determine what kind of actions one considers to be morally laudable, whether one thinks that the NGO’s are morally justified to do what they do or whether they are not justified.

Divine Command Theory versus Natural Law Theory: This is the issue of how morality is justified from religious points of view. Commonly, in Christianity and other religions, morality is justified by either the argument that something is good because God wills it so (many Protestant Christians justify morality in this fashion). Or, else, it is justified because it is in line with the order of nature, whereas nature is God’s creation (thus, perfect or, at least, very good; many Catholics justify their morality in this fashion).

Possible examples: Standard examples are that Natural Law Theory has problems with accepting homosexuality (because sexuality’s goal is procreation and homosexuality does not fit this bill) and that Divine Command Theory rules out e.g. euthanasia (because it is against God’s will). Examples like these (and/or related ones) will be discussed. The question will also be raised as to whether Divine Command Theory and Natural Law Theory are the only ways to justify morality from a religious (Christian) point of view or whether there are religions or streams within particular religions which justify their morality in a different fashion. Religious morality will not only be looked at from Christian but also form related religious, e.g. Islamic, viewpoints.

Teaching Methods:
The course synthesizes practical issues with the theoretical reflection on it. It will utilize the case studies-method according to which specific moral issues are discussed in light of different ethical theories. It will demonstrate to what extent moral theory and practice are interlinked and that responsible moral decision-making always entails serious theoretical reflections (and, by the same token, that doing moral theorizing without having concrete cases in mind is futile). The sessions will usually begin with an introduction into a particular theory and then be followed by an application of this theory to a practical case and this case wil be evaluated in light of a the theory. The cases to be chosen will be determined by the students (for examples, see above). All students are expected to be present at the sessions.

Course Objective:
This course offers a critical anthropological examination of international development, with a focus on decolonial perspectives. Students engage with key theories and practices of development, globalisation and decolonisation, and analyse the historical, political and sociocultural dimensions of development processes at multiple scales. The course equips students with analytical tools to critically assess development discourses, their assumptions and their effects on governance, inequality and lived experience.

Course Content:
This course looks from an anthropological perspective at the interrelated themes of develop-ment and globalization. We will analyse “development” as concept, discourse, and assemblage of practices, looking at their local and global effects. We will untangle how different actors—governments, supranational agencies, NGOs, multinational corporations, activists, local populations, etc.—interact and negotiate in development processes, with special attention to power asymmetries and socioeconomic inequalities. We also highlight potential and experienced gaps between intentions and outcomes of development policies and look at what anthropology can contribute to “development” debates and policy implementation. And, finally, while studying development, we also seek to grasp what globalization actually is and does—and, likewise, what it is not.

Teaching Methods:
The course consists of lectures which will include group discussion activities. Students are expected to follow (and actively participate in) these lectures and activities, to which mandatory readings are required to be done beforehand in order to ensure participation in discussions.

Method of Assessment:
Book club reflections

Students are expected to come to class having done the required readings and be able to discuss their content. In addition, students submit a written reflection (70-100 words) on a highlight of the chapters, through Canvas. Based on the readings, the reflection can be a commentary, further questions for discussion, or connections with other texts (of the course) or current news.

Exam

The digital exam consists of two parts: Part I: 20 multiple-choice questions (50% of the grade). Part II: Two open-ended questions requiring an essay-like response (50% of the grade). Exam questions will draw from the literature, lectures, and discussions. Students will be able to answer the questions if they keep up with the readings (including of the book club) and attend the lectures.

Part II of the exam will be assessed according to two criteria, with equal weight: 1) Correct use of ideas and concepts according to the course materials; and 2) Quality of the argument, originality and critical reflection.

The multiple-choice part of the exam uses guess correction (formula scoring) for multiple-choice exams, in accordance with faculty policy.

Course Objective:
This course introduces students to the theory and practice of visual and audiovisual anthropology. Students examine key debates about image, representation and knowledge production, and develop practical skills in designing and realising small audiovisual ethnographic projects. Ethical reflection on issues of representation, consent and positionality runs throughout the course. The course broadens students' multimodal repertoire and deepens their understanding of non-textual forms of ethnographic communication.

Course Content:
Image and sound are increasingly being implemented in both academic and applied research, also in anthropology. It is now difficult to imagine doing qualitative research without incorporating the virtual lives of our interlocutors, or, more practically, without a smartphone that captures sound and image instantly. Besides text, anthropologists now increasingly produce audiovisual media about their ethnographic findings from the field. By turning image and sound into documentaries and essay films, photo essays, or (virtual) art installations, they actively challenge the limits of academic representation. These new developments are shaping our methodologies and our ways of crafting knowledge. But audiovisual anthropology is not new. The gathering of audiovisual material and the audiovisual representation of ethnographic data have a prevailing history in anthropology.

In this course, we will explore the history and variety of audiovisual approaches in anthropology and analyse how different forms of image and sound work as tools for cultural exchange, theorizing, and situated understanding. In the course, we will also investigate in detail the role of positionality of film makers in the way film is being made as well as our own positionality as a viewer and a maker. Specifically, we will watch and analyse new and classical work in anthropological filmmaking and students will collectively produce a short film. The course therefore not only deals with theory on audiovisual representations, but also on the practical dilemmas and the ethical concerns of ‘doing’ audiovisual ethnography.

Teaching Methods:
Interactive lectures, film viewings, practical labs, group discussions

Method of Assessment:
One final exam (individual); one short audiovisual project with a written assignment (collective)

Literature:

Course Objective:
This elective course examines gender inequalities through an intersectional and interdisciplinary lens. Students engage with key theories and debates from gender studies and cognate fields, and apply these frameworks to complex, real-world problems. Through collaborative research and teamwork, students develop skills in interdisciplinary analysis, critical reflection and translating academic knowledge into actionable insights for external stakeholders.

Course Content:
Gender is everywhere in our lives, in our society, and in the world. There is nothing in this world that isn’t related to gender in one way or another. It’s in everything we do. From the clothes we wear and the way we sit, to whether we feel safe walking outside at night and how much we earn through our employment, to the likelihood of us becoming prime minister and the kind of healthcare we will get.

In Beyond Gender Inequalities, we move beyond simple categorisations, and explore the complexity of gender. We move beyond the gender binary: beyond binary concepts of identities, bodies, and behaviours such as men and women, male and female, and masculine and feminine. We ask: where do these binaries come from, are they the reality of how we live our lives, why do they have such a strong hold on us, and what are the consequences of organising gender in binary ways? We also move beyond gender as a singular category of analysis: we argue that in order to understand gender, it is not enough to simply look at gender by itself, because gender is intimately connected to various other systems of privilege and marginalisation such as race, sexuality, class, disability and age, which affect and shape how gender is experienced and lived, and therefore how it can be analysed.

In other words, the course argues that gender equity goes beyond an ‘add and stir’ approach: resolving gendered issues requires more than merely increasing the numbers of individuals from different gender minorities within organisations, institutions, and companies, or developing diversity policies. It requires a fundamental rethinking of how power operates structurally. This course, then, breaks binary thinking wide open. It proposes an analysis of complex gendered issues from intersectional lenses that move beyond Eurocentric, heteronormative definitions and individualising and marketised approaches, and supports students in developing an intellectual and affective understanding of gender as a site where race, class, sexuality, and other identity markers intersect.

This critical approach to gender, while challenging, facilitates an analysis of gendered inequities and injustices in a way that reflects more accurately the situation, positions, and experiences of people and communities who are marginalised and excluded from dominant normative frameworks. It also enables the study of those in power, those who are included in and considered the social norm. It In order to understand and fight gendered inequities, both the positions of those who are marginalised and those who are privileged must be addressed, including their interactions.

This course is taught by a team of teachers with backgrounds in intersectional gender studies, sociology, political science, organisation science, communication science, anthropology, and disability studies, which is key in fostering a sensibility for interdisciplinary thinking.

The course is structured around the following two key questions:

How can intersectional approaches help us understand and resolve complex gendered problems in our society?

How can societal and organisational structures truly integrate principles of gender equity and social justice?

Teaching Methods:
Delivery mode

The course is made up of lectures and tutorials. The interactive lectures are scheduled in weeks 1 to 3, and engage with various theoretical, methodological, and disciplinary perspectives on gender-related issues and in intersectional gender studies. By attending the lectures, students develop a strong foundation of conceptual and analytical tools that allows them to connect theoretical concepts to complex societal challenges in an interdisciplinary fashion.

The tutorials take place in weeks 2 to 7. In addition to providing a space for discussion of the lecture and reading materials, the tutorials’ main purpose is to support students in the development of the major assignment in the course, creating a (maga)zine. Students work together in groups to analyse a specific case study related to a complex gender issue, and publish their findings in a (maga)zine. This (maga)zine will contain both individually written articles as well as a group-written introduction and afterword. For the (maga)zine, students are encouraged to blend conventional academic writing with less conventional or alternative forms of writing. Layout and presentation are also important. In week 3, students take part in a zine-making workshop.

Attendance

Attendance and active participation in tutorials are mandatory. Students can miss one tutorial but must notify their tutor of their absence. More than one missed tutorial may result in a substitute assignment.

Attendance at lectures is required to be able to successfully complete the assignments.

Method of Assessment:
Assessment consists of an individual written assignment; a group (maga)zine, which includes individual writing, group writing, and a presentation; and participation in tutorials.

In order to pass the course, students must receive a passing grade or Sufficient evaluation for every graded assignment.

Graded assignments for which students have not received a passing grade or a Sufficient evaluation must be resubmitted either during the course or during the resit period.
